title: What the heck is going on with Browns DE Jared Verse?
summary: The Cleveland Browns are at a threshold. They can continue their winning ways, or plunder and waste the season. The loss to the New York Jets shows that either they had a bad game or they just aren’t a very good team. The Jets were a definite “ schedule W” for the Browns, and they […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns are at a threshold. They can continue their winning ways, or plunder and waste the season. The loss to the New York Jets shows that either they had a bad game or they just aren’t a very good team. The Jets were a definite “ schedule W” for the Browns, and they are not a good team. The loss could cripple the franchise’s season and could send it into an abyss instead of a continued upward spiral. RELATED: CAN JARED VERSE ACTIVATE BEAST MODE? Along this journey, the defense has done its job in almost every game. Right now, Cleveland’s defense is ranked #20 overall, giving up an average of 334 yards a game. They are ranked #13 versus the pass and #19 against the run. The Browns have the fourth-most sacks with 16. One defensive player has so far been omitted from this category: DE Jared Verse. Cleveland shipped off their best pass rusher when they traded Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams. Along with a handful of draft picks, the Browns received Verse. It was stated that the Cleveland GM, Andrew Berry, would not make the trade without Verse included, so the Rams agreed. Verse came with lots of accolades and a sense of potential. He has been in the league only two years and was voted to the Pro Bowl each season. As a rookie, he won the “NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year” award after gathering 4.5 sacks, 18 QB hits, 33 pressures, and 66 total tackles, among other stats. Last year, he had 7.5 sacks and 36 pressures. For 2026? Something is off. Right now, Verse has yet to register a sack at all. He has started all five games, and yet has just 13 total tackles. 2.6 tackles a game on average seems a bit light, given that he has to defend an entire edge. Maybe teams aren’t running his way towards the left flats. Maybe? Pro Football Focus has given him a 67.3 run defense grade and ranked him #35 among qualified edge rushers. So, he is getting the job done when the ball is being carried in his direction. Or at least making the ball carrier turn it upfield before they attempt to sweep outside. He does have three tackles for loss. But it’s the pass rush, or lack thereof, that is concerning regarding Verse. He isn’t getting much penetration from his left defensive end position. And it’s not like teams are double-teaming him, although there are plenty of snaps where a tight end will either chip him or remain along the line to assist the right tackle. Verse’s stats so far this year: five starts, 13 total tackles, 3 tackles for loss, 0 fumble recoveries, 0 forced fumbles, 4 QB hits, 0 batted passes, 0 sacks, 2 knockdowns, 0 hurries, 2 pressures, and 3 missed tackles. Perhaps part of his lack of production this year is centered around the fact that he really is considered a part-time player. So far, Verse has played on 224 snaps, which is 66% of all defensive reps. His backup, Sam Williams, has played on 120 snaps, or 35% of all defensive plays. But Williams has more tackles (15), sacks (1), and batted passes (1), plus the same number of tackles for loss (3), pressures (2), and missed tackles (3). Verse was the centerpiece of the Garrett trade. He was supposed to come in and get double-digit sack numbers and wreak havoc on opponents when they dropped back to pass. He is younger than Garrett, so the Browns would retain a more youthful, prototypical pass-rushing demon. Yet his run-stopping numbers are pretty good, and his pass-rushing figures stink. Nobody has asked Verse to become Myles Garrett 2.0, but the expectations were pretty high that he would provide this Cleveland defense with a stiff pass rush. None of that has shown through the first five games. His numbers have plenty to be desired. His strength was his intensity. But maybe he is trying to do too much. Perhaps being the key pawn in the Garrett sits on him to become great, and that is getting in the way. Focus on his game, and not the game that is expected of him. Needless to say, Verse is struggling. Verse’s stats game-by-game: Tackles/sacks/QB hits Jaguars: 4-0-0 Buccaneers: 1-0-1 Panthers: 3-0-1 Steelers: 2-0-0 Jets: 3-0-2 Now, the flip side is that Verse is perhaps aiding other defensive players. The defensive tackle on Verse’s side, Maliek Collins, has 2.5 sacks. Perhaps Verse helped collapse the pocket so that a quarterback tried to escape and found Collins instead. That is often how defenses work. A stunt will require one player to become congested with two offensive linemen while his line mate sweeps around with an open lane. Or a blitz is called sending the safety around the edge, and it is Verse’s job to remain engaged with the offensive tackle. His goose egg in the sack department is concerning. At times, he does not contain, and opposing ball carriers have found large gains and even scored because nobody is home. Another reason for the abrupt change is that while with the Rams, Verse played an outside linebacker role in a 3-4 scheme and now is asked to attack as a 4-3 defensive end in Cleveland. DC Mike Rutenberg stated that Verse maintained that his overall disruption goes beyond raw sack numbers. In the postgame press conference after the Jets game, Rutenberg stated regarding Verse: “First of all, I think (Verse) is doing a great job. When you look at games, everybody is looking for the ‘ooh’ and the ‘wow’ play. That’s not what defense is. Defense is about violence, violence, chaos, disruption, and getting the ball. And it’s 11 dudes hunting on defense. And he’s hunting on defense. And somebody might ‘ooh’ and ‘ah, a great pick, but go watch the tape. Jared Verse might be disrupting the quarterback on that play. I’m going to go back to the Tampa Bay game where he chased it down from the backside. That’s what defense is about. It’s creating chaos and disruption, and he’s doing that.” Certainly, defense is a team effort. And sometimes one guy has a great play that another player will get the credit for or increase his stats. But Verse is an outside pass rusher. His journey is pretty clear on most plays. On passing downs, he either gets pressure on the other team’s quarterback, or he doesn’t. It’s not just one thing. It’s not even just about pressure. Collectively, the defense wants to make the quarterback uncomfortable and lessen his time to throw. The Browns’ entire goal is to place players in the best position and allow their style to come through. And maybe this year is Verse’s time to assist other defensive players in shining. Possibly he is having an off year. Or perhaps he just isn’t getting the job done. What do you think about Jared Verse’s start with the Browns? Join the conversation! title: Brian Schottenheimer report card: Todd Bowles dominates Cowboys head coach in week 5
summary: It was bound to happen, we just did not think it would come in Week 5 against the 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers. For the first time this season, despite a 2-2 start, play-caller Brian Schottenheimer was absolutely dominated on game day. If you’re unfamiliar with Todd Bowles defenses, it all relies on exotic blitz looks […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It was bound to happen, we just did not think it would come in Week 5 against the 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers. For the first time this season, despite a 2-2 start, play-caller Brian Schottenheimer was absolutely dominated on game day. If you’re unfamiliar with Todd Bowles defenses, it all relies on exotic blitz looks and simulated pressure. That’s exactly what the Cowboys offense saw on Thursday night, and they never came up with an answer on how to beat it. In the first half, the Cowboys offense had some offensive success, but struggled to get into third and manageable, leading to far too many third-and-longs. That played right into Bowles hands, as he was able to mix up blitz looks to scheme pressure on quarterback Dak Prescott. In the first half, the route concepts the Cowboys were calling against the Buccaneers blitz looks left a lot to be desired. The Cowboys faced far too many 3rd and 7+ and that led to far too many long developing routes. In most cases against heavy pressure, you’d love to have a few receivers at or past the sticks, and safety valves to get the ball out to with a chance to pick up the first down after the catch (Javonte Williams was fantastic in pass protection). That was nonexistent for most of the night leading to a lot of incompletions, tight window throws, and some errant throws from Dak Prescott. With the scheme making it hard on the Cowboys passing and running game, we saw a season high in punts (three) and only converting on four of 10 third downs in their 24-16 loss. Even with the schematic issues in the Cowboys week five loss, they had an opportunity to win the game, but two dropped passes resulting in interceptions, along with a KaVontae Turpin fumble on the Cowboys second possession of the second half, killed any momentum and hope of the Cowboys winning the game. It’s unfair we ask the offense to be near perfect week in-and-week out, but with the way the defense has played over the last year-and-a-half, they will need to be. For a coach that has been in the league calling plays for 20 years, he needs to be better. It was very disappointing to see Bowles out-coach Schottenheimer at the rate that he did on Thursday night, and the conversation would have been just as loud if the Cowboys were able to pull off the comeback. With the division still wide open, Schottenheimer has to consider making changes on the offensive side of the ball. A few to consider would be cutting into Jake Ferguson’s reps, considering more route concepts and play calls that target the middle of the field, and using a bit more of Tyler Goodson in the underneath passing game (did not receive a carry or target in week five) to get some quick, easy completions with a more explosive runner after the catch. While it sounds like there are changes coming to the defensive side of the ball, Schottenheimer should not be cleared of criticism, even with the offensive performing at a very high-level for four out of the Cowboys five games so far in 2026. Play-Calling F Fourth-Down Decisions N/A The Cowboys only went for it on one fourth down in week five. An incompletion on a rushed throw from Prescott was the result. All other fourth downs were six plus yards and given the Cowboys struggles on offense, the decision to go would have been way too risky. Timeout Usage N/A Team Preparation F It was all pretty ugly. What grade would you give to Brian Schottenheimer on Sunday?

Obviously last week was not a good one for the Dallas Cowboys so power rankings aren’t going to be fun. Let’s get to them anyway. 1 – San Francisco 49ers (LW: 1) They look unstoppable right now. If the Cowboys do wind up getting it together they will at some poine likely have to go through their boogeyman. 2 – Buffalo Bills (LW: 4) They are clearly the AFC’s best at the moment. 3 – Kansas City Chiefs (LW: 2) Welcome back from the bye. They are definitely hanging around. 11 – Chicago Bears (LW: 7) The loss was tough, but it is impossible to truly evaluate them until Caleb Williams is back. 12 – Denver Broncos (LW: 11) They are so clearly held back by their quarterback. But wins are wins. 13 – Los Angeles Rams (LW: 8) 2-3 just like the Cowboys. And their head coach is a big reason why, too. 14 – Atlanta Falcons (LW: 13) Obviously they lost, but the Falcons have a spunk to them. I’m intrigued. 15 – Carolina Panthers (LW: 14) The NFC South might belong to the Panthers again, though. 16 – Green Bay Packers (LW: 22) See you Sunday. Be gentle. 17 – Pittsburgh Steelers (LW: 24) Mike McCarthy is making lemonade. Good for him. 18 – New York Giants (LW: 18) I’d imagine we all agree that they have a pretty low ceiling this year given the injuries, but they deserve so much credit for actually reaching it. They are clearly not the Giants of old. 19 – Dallas Cowboys (LW: 12) Every time we give them an inch of trust… they burn us. 20 – Philadelphia Eagles (LW: 15) The vibes are quite poor here. 21 – Las Vegas Raiders (LW: 17) Even though they lost, I still feel like they are headed in the right direction. Things just take time. 22 – Houston Texans (LW: 26) It is going to be awesome to see Marvin Harrison Jr. with C.J. Stroud. 23 – Indianapolis Colts (LW: 19) What do the Colts do well? Anything? 24 – Cleveland Browns (LW: 21) Back to earth. 25 – Tampa Bay Buccaneers (LW: 29) Kudos to them for exposing the Cowboys. 26 – New Orleans Saints (LW: 23) When the offense is on it is so awesome. The rest of the team is just… not good. 27 – New York Jets (LW: 28) A win is a win! 28 – Washington Commanders (LW: 25) Jayden Daniels not knowing the timeout situation is such an indictment. Everybody involved failed. 29 – Arizona Cardinals (LW: 27) They are going to beat the Cowboys, aren’t they? 30 – Los Angeles Chargers (LW: 30) Yikes. 31 – Miami Dolphins (LW: 32) Double yikes. 32 – Tennessee Titans (LW: 31) I’m not sure they are actually an NFL team. ESPN : 15 (LW: 12) So it begins. Biggest issue on defense: Everything? How do you pick just one issue when it comes to the Cowboys? They are giving up 27.2 points per game, which ranks 26th in the NFL. They are giving up 168.4 rushing yards per game, which is last in the league. They have recorded only five sacks and do not have an interception this season. Opposing quarterbacks are completing 72.3% of their passes. Through five games, new coordinator Christian Parker’s defense might not be worse than it was under Matt Eberflus last season. But it is at least the same and a big reason why Dallas is 2-3. — Todd Archer NFL.com : 18 (LW: 8) A sizable drop. The Cowboys suffered a disastrous loss on Thursday night, falling to a previously winless Buccaneers team that had every reason to lay down in Arlington. Instead, Bucky Irving ran through Dallas’ defense, Jalon Daniels produced a creditable performance in place of Baker Mayfield, and the Cowboys’ typically-explosive offense mustered just 16 points. We know Dallas only has one path to victory — light up the scoreboard — and when that doesn’t work, it exposes the flaws in this club. It’s only one loss, but it eliminated much of my confidence in this team being a real contender. USA Today : 24 (LW: 18) And again. The Cowboys are 32nd in defensive DVOA, the exact spot they held last season. title: Mike Pettine could have a bigger influence on defense than advertised
summary: Before Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer left the podium Thursday night after the embarrassing loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, he said the team is being evaluated at all levels for potential change. After the mini-bye week, Dallas made a big change, or more specifically addition. The team is hiring long-time NFL coach Mike […]
full_text: Photo by Tom Hauck/Getty Images Before Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer left the podium Thursday night after the embarrassing loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, he said the team is being evaluated at all levels for potential change. After the mini-bye week, Dallas made a big change, or more specifically addition. The team is hiring long-time NFL coach Mike Pettine as a senior defensive assistant . Pettine was one of Christian Parker’s mentors during his time with the Green Bay Packers, so the two know each other. When Parker was hired in Dallas, Todd Archer spoke with Pettine about what he learned about Parker, who was 28 at the time, while they worked together. “From the jump, when you spend time around him, you realize he’s much more mature than what his age is, especially from a football standpoint,” Pettine said. “He had a lot of good input but didn’t force it on the room. He and I spent a lot of time together because he would do the game-plan drawings. If we had an issue with a formation or a defense we put together, he had input and he’s not just doing the drawing. You’re recognizing pretty quickly there’s an ‘it,’ factor with him.” “There were certain things I wanted from him that would be hard to see from the sideline, and he was always good with those things,” Pettine said. “He was good at ‘What can we do?’ and ‘What can’t we do?’ Again, he was a QC with us, but he definitely had my ear.” With the Cowboys’ defense sitting last in many categories over a month into the season, they looked outside the building for a former mentor to bring a new voice to the room. Parker wanted to bring Pettine on as a consultant after he was hired, but the former defensive coordinator wanted to stay retired. There was an open invitation to jump on board. Now that the invitation has been checked “yes,” the Cowboys have someone to help guide Parker through the rest of the season and help the young coordinator regain his footing that made him a qualified candidate in the first place. Ed Werder adds context, suggesting Pettine could end up with a bigger voice in the room than the team is presenting. The #Cowboys are carefully representing the hiring of Pettine as someone who is here to support Christian Parker and offer advice based on his experience. But NFL coaches I’ve spoken to who know Pettine and the dynamics of the situation with the Cowboys believe the more influence… pic.twitter.com/A5bk3wxpN6 — Ed Werder (@WerderEdNFL) October 13, 2026 In the days since Thursday night’s loss, Jerry Jones and Schottenheimer have reaffirmed their belief in Parker as the guy to lead their defense. Outside of letting go of Parker, this was the right move for the Cowboys. It comes at a good time because, with the Green Bay Packers coming up this weekend, Pettine’s last two years in the NFL were spent with Matt LaFleur and the Packers. The NFC East is up for the taking. The Philadelphia Eagles are on a three-game losing streak, the New York Giants might not sustain the Jameis Winston magic for long, and the Washington Commanders look on the verge of breaking. If Pettine gets more of a voice in defensive meetings and takes some responsibility off Parker’s shoulders, applaud the Cowboys for making a move to improve their team and address a desperate need. Parker’s specialty is with the secondary, so maybe with Pettine in the building, Parker can spend more time with DaRon Bland and others to help improve the league’s worst defense in EPA per play .

title: Will Cowboys be buyers or sellers at the November 10 NFL trade deadline?
summary: With the NFC East completely wide open, don’t be surprised if Jerry Jones is looking to make another big move to improve the Dallas Cowboys chances of winning the division. He is a known gambler and sitting on his hands and letting things play out is simply not his style. He’s more of a “damn […]
full_text: Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images | Getty Images With the NFC East completely wide open, don’t be surprised if Jerry Jones is looking to make another big move to improve the Dallas Cowboys chances of winning the division. He is a known gambler and sitting on his hands and letting things play out is simply not his style. He’s more of a “damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead” type of person, and that attitude could come in to play with the November 10 NFL trade deadline approaching. Between now and the trade deadline the Cowboys have four games to play against the Green Bay Packers, Philadelphia Eagles, Arizona Cardinals, and the Indianapolis Colts. Depending on how those games turn out, especially against the Eagles, could determine whether they are buyers like they have been this year or sellers to help reload for next year and beyond. Today, we’ll at both sides of the argument. Buyers Jerry Jones has shown little hesitancy parting with future draft capital this year. He already traded for Rashan Gary, Dee Winters, Broderick Jones, and most recently Joey Porter Jr. As a result, they currently only have a total of four picks in the 2026 NFL Draft, one in the first, second, fourth, and seventh rounds. Despite that, Jerry Jones insists he’s more than willing to sacrifice the future to upgrade the present. If true, the Cowboys could very well be buyers once again. Maxx Crosby continues to be rumored as a trade target for them, and fellow pass rusher Josh Sweat is another name thrown around, especially after the way the Cardinal season is circling the drain. To acquire either one of them via trade would likely take at least Dallas’ first-round pick next year with some change thrown in, further depleting next year’s draft capital. It’s certainly not out of the realm of possibility, but may be unwise considering how the Cowboys are currently struggling defensively and not playing up to their talent on the offensive side of the ball. Yes, it may result in a playoff berth, but another early exit without the tools to rebuild for the future could hurt the organization for a number of years. It would be another risk for Jerry Jones among many since purchasing the team. Sellers Depending on how the next four games play out for the Cowboys, it may make sense for them to start selling off their best trade assets to the highest bidder. Next year’s draft class is a talented one, especially at positions of “need” for Dallas. They are a team that has been building through the draft for a number of years now and stocking up on more draft capital could be in the best interest for the future of the organization. The Cowboys have a number of trade assets who could be appealing to other teams around the league. George Pickens of course is at the top of the list. He could net them some high-round draft capital, but the limitations, because of the franchise tag, on signing a new contract with a new team hurts that value some. T.J. Bass could have some serious suitors as well, among others Dallas could be willing to part ways with. Being sellers ahead of the November 10 trade deadline this year makes a lot of sense based on how things are playing out for the Cowboys so far this season. Right now there is no reason to believe this team can make waves in the playoffs. It may actually make more sense to reload and try again next year. That, of course, depends on how Jerry Jones and Company view things. He may be more optimistic things can still be turned around. The game at the Packers on Sunday will be telling. What do you think? Will the Cowboys be buyers or sellers at the trade deadline?

title: Brian Schottenheimer is keeping poor company right now
summary: It has only been 22 games, to be clear. But right now Brian Schottenheimer is in some poor company. The company in question is as things relate to Dallas Cowboys franchise history. Schottenheimer has led the team through a full season and five games of another, and in both instances he failed to win a […]
full_text: Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images | Getty Images It has only been 22 games, to be clear. But right now Brian Schottenheimer is in some poor company. The company in question is as things relate to Dallas Cowboys franchise history. Schottenheimer has led the team through a full season and five games of another, and in both instances he failed to win a majority of his first five games. This isn’t an arbitrary mark chosen, to be clear. Stathead and Pro Football Reference only allow searching spans to begin a season that are at least five games in length, and now that the Cowboys are through that point we can really measure Schottenheimer against those who came before him. Here is every team in Dallas Cowboys franchise history to hold two or fewer wins through their first five games. This specific wording allows us to capture the tie from Week 5 last year. The Cowboys have held two or fewer wins through five games a total of 24 times now. They made the playoffs only twice in the previous 23 instances. Not great. What is interesting is if we consider the head coaches who, like Brian Schottenheimer, did this in consecutive seasons. It is quite (not really) the list. Dallas Cowboys head coaches to lead the team to two or fewer wins through the first five games in consecutive seasons: Brian Schottenheimer Jason Garrett Dave Campo Jimmy Johnson Tom Landry Again, apologies for the specific wording. 2-2-1 is not the same thing as 2-3, but I think we all agree that in an effective sense it is. Moving on. Brian Schottenheimer is either going to be Jason Garrett or Dave Campo… or Jimmy Johnson or Tom Landry. Based on this at least. Many will likely say that the reason the latter pair dealt with starts of this variety is because of the day and age they played in as well as the fact that when they each took over they did so when the franchise was at very low points. That is more than fair. Briain Schottenheimer hardly inherited an expansion team or one with the number one overall pick. Things are taking on water in a very serious sense for the Cowboys right now and if Schottenheimer doesn’t sort them out then he really is going to be associated with names that people do not regard all too fondly. Time is running out.

title: Cowboys news: Team adds defensive help to coaching staff
summary: The Dallas Cowboys losing on Thursday night at home to the previously winless Buccaneers was somehow not the most embarrassing thing to happen throughout the NFC East in week five. The Philadelphia Eagles had their own international meltdown involving a late field goal to lose, in London to the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Commanders ran the […]
full_text: Photo by Dylan Buell/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys losing on Thursday night at home to the previously winless Buccaneers was somehow not the most embarrassing thing to happen throughout the NFC East in week five. The Philadelphia Eagles had their own international meltdown involving a late field goal to lose, in London to the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Commanders ran the clock out on themselves with a chance to beat the first place New York Giants in overtime. The 2-3 Cowboys are still in the playoff race as a result, but they need to avoid further coaching mistakes like the rest of their rivals. The organization hired Mike Pettine to help first year defensive coordinator Christian Parker on Monday to help with this. Cowboys add Mike Pettine to defensive coaching staff – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com The Cowboys had visions of Christian Parker working with veteran coach Mike Pettine for some time, and hired the former Packers coach ahead of a primetime game in Green Bay. Mike Pettine has been added as senior defensive assistant — a former defensive coordinator of the New York Jets, Buffalo Bills and the Green Bay Packers, and he most recently worked with the Minnesota Vikings to help Brian Flores form one of the more formidable defenses in the league. “Had a chance to work with Pettine for a number of years, along with the Jets, and he’s gonna be here in a role to support everything that [Christian Parker] is leading and guiding, and we are really, really excited,” Schottenheimer said on Monday. “They worked together in Green Bay, and this is actually something the C.P. and I talked about when we first hired him.” What a horrific NFL week 5 for the NFC East – Shane Tayl0r, Inside The Star Kickoff strategy in late-game situations will be a real discussion point between the Cowboys and Eagles, who play each other in Week 7. A 48-yard field goal for Philly gave them a 19-17 lead with eight seconds remaining. However, Jags returner Ameer Abdullah returned the ensuing kickoff 53 yards to set up Cam Little with a 57-yard field goal. So, instead of kicking the ball into the end zone, forcing the Jags to have to run a play on offense with no timeouts, head coach of the Eagles, Nick Sirianni, kept it in play and allowed legit the only thing that could have beat you happen. NFL Week 5 Sunday aftermath: Commanders melt down in tie; Eagles rue costly last-second gaffe – Kevin Patra, NFL.com Nick Sirianni took the blame for the Eagles late loss the same way Brian Schottenheimer did after Thursday night. Sirianni likely had the Week 3 Ravens-Cowboys ending in his brain at the time, wherein Dallas kicked to the end zone, which allowed Baltimore to run a play and get into field goal range in six seconds for a stunning game-winner . The difference here was that Jacksonville didn’t have a timeout. That detail is massive. Without a timeout, even starting at the 35-yard line, Jacksonville would have had to throw at a presumably well-guarded boundary to stop the clock. Not impossible, but harder than the helter-skelter kick returns can create. That Philly allowed a big return that was called back to start the game — and was missing a key special teams player in Jeremiah Trotter Jr. , who earlier was ejected for fighting — should also have played a role in Sirianni’s thinking. Download the SB Nation app today! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . After slow growth, Cowboys defense struggles vs lowly Bucs – Dyllan Rivers, Blogging The Boys The way the Cowboys allowed explosive plays against the Bucs in the second half was highly concerning. On the first play of the second half, Bucky Irving broke free on a run that seemed to take an eternity to cross the line of scrimmage, finally taken down by Caleb Downs after a 72-yard scamper. The very next play resulted in a Tampa Bay touchdown. Two plays, 86 yards, seven points. The next drive, coming after a Ryan Flournoy tipped ball interception, blew open on a Tez Johnson 64-yard catch and run. DaRon Bland tripped over his own feet, allowing Johnson to run free deep into Cowboys territory. After three back-to-back run plays, the Buccaneers would go on to score another touchdown. Enough time has passed for us to point out the 3 silver linings from the Dallas Cowboys’ loss to the Bucs in Week 5 – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports CeeDee Lamb was quiet in the Thursday night home game, but it meant George Pickens finally got going. Is Dallas closer to having both receivers go off in the same game? No one should have been overly concerned. This is the way the Cowboys offense will operate as long as it has two elite wide receivers. Still, a strong performance from Pickens is good for everyone in Dallas, and mostly for his confidence. He finished with nine catches for 130 yards and a touchdown on 13 targets. The Cowboys went to him on the slant a lot once again. He probably wants a few of those targets back, but beyond the numbers, Pickens kept showing up when the Cowboys needed him the most.

title: Broncos vs. Seahawks: 3 Players to Watch in Week 6
summary: The stakes are high when the Denver Broncos host the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football. Finding a way to topple the defending Super Bowl champions is going to be extremely difficult. Here are three players that need to perform at a high level in order for Denver to earn their fourth victory of the […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Santa Clara, California, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) during the third quarter against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The stakes are high when the Denver Broncos host the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football . Finding a way to topple the defending Super Bowl champions is going to be extremely difficult. Here are three players that need to perform at a high level in order for Denver to earn their fourth victory of the season. Riley Moss — Cornerback On a short week, it’s still uncertain if Riley Moss is going to play on Thursday Night Football . He has been limited in Denver’s practice sessions thus far. We will probably know much more sometime this afternoon in that respect. In the event he doesn’t, you can just throw in “Whoever is tasked with covering Jaxon Smith-Njigba” here instead. The Broncos have faced some really good offenses to start the season. In my mind, there is no doubt Smith-Njigba is the premier playmaker for the Seahawks on offense. He is the reigning Offensive Player of the Year. The star wide receiver already has four 100 receiving yard performances this season, seven touchdowns, and is on pace to shatter the career best numbers he put up last in 2025. Denver’s banged up secondary will be without Patrick Surtain II and Talanoa Hufanga. That will make it even harder to limit Smith-Njigba’s impact. If Moss is a go, I expect most of that responsibility to be on his shoulders. The savvy wideout can beat you deep and he can create after the catch. He’s one of the most well-rounded receivers in the NFL. I’m very interested to see what kind of coverage plan Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph has in store to keep him from having a huge game. Jaylen Waddle — Wide Receiver The Broncos traded multiple premium picks to add Jaylen Waddle to their receiving corps. The hope was that the sixth-year wideout would be an impact player for the team and take their passing attack to new heights. Unfortunately, Waddle has been missing in action for most of the season. Outside of the Broncos’ Week 2 win versus the Jacksonville Jaguars where he had eight catches for 138 yards, the sixth-year wideout hasn’t made much of an impact. He has just 18 catches for 204 yards and 1 touchdown. Through five games, Waddle is sporting the worst catch percentage of his career at 58-percent. The Seahawks have been phenomenal shutting down opposing team’s passing attacks. Even so, this is a game where Waddle has to make an impact for the Broncos. They invested a lot of resources to acquire him, and the early returns aren’t too great. Can he rebound and be a difference maker in primetime? Denver will need that to happen to be victorious. Bo Nix — Quarterback It’s been a slow start to Bo Nix’s third season as the starting quarterback of the Broncos. I’m quite honestly surprised. I felt he was poised for a big jump in productivity and efficiency. Unfortunately, the results thus far aren’t great. In four of five games, Nix has thrown for less than 215 yards. Four of those contests have resulted in a completion percentage below at or below 60-percent. He has also had a turnover in four of five games. He has one of the worst EPA ranking for any quarterback in the NFL. The Seahawks sport a very good defense. They force turnovers, are fantastic on third down, and are allowing just 150 yards per game through the air. This will be a very tough game for Nix to get back on track. However, the Broncos desperately need a spark and much better play from their third-year signal caller. Can he hit some concepts over the middle of the field? Will he be able to find a few big plays down the field like he did often during the ’25 season? I have no idea if that transpires. If it does, I really like Denver’s chances of winning. Most importantly, I also think a good performance would give him a much-needed boost of confidence. I don’t expect an elite performance, but I want to see a good outing from Bo on Thursday Night Football .

title: Two issues on offense are holding the Broncos back
summary: This might surprise a lot of people, but one of those issues is not quarterback Bo Nix. In watching this offense it has become pretty clear that the passing game is being disrupted by Nix’s lack of trust in the interior line where Ben Powers and Luke Wattenberg are mostly responsible in pass protection. He […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 24: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos takes a snap as Ben Powers #74 blocks during the fourth quarter of a game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on November 24, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images This might surprise a lot of people, but one of those issues is not quarterback Bo Nix. In watching this offense it has become pretty clear that the passing game is being disrupted by Nix’s lack of trust in the interior line where Ben Powers and Luke Wattenberg are mostly responsible in pass protection. He bailed away from that side of the line whether there is pressure there or not. A change there would be good, but that never seems to happen. I went and looked at 2025 also and found four of Nix’s five 295+ passing yard games came during the stretch of games when Powers was on injured reserve. Just something to look for moving forward. Maybe it’s not Bo Nix, but a protection issue. The second one is getting Jonah Coleman healthy. J.K. Dobbins had a few decent runs late in Sunday’s game, but he was wholly ineffective for much of that game. It just seemed like he has no juice left. Getting into some better second and third down and distances would also be huge for this offense. Fixing one or both of these issues would go a long way towards all of us enjoying the offensive gameplay each week. That’s my feeling about the offense right now. There are other issues, to be sure, but I believe if they can get these two fixed then the offense as a whole can overcome the rest. What do you think? Let me have it in the comments! title: Broncos vs. Seahawks: 3 Things to Watch in Week 6
summary: The Denver Broncos host the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football. Earlier today, I discussed how the Broncos can earn their fourth win of the season. Now, I’ll turn my focus to three major storylines I’ll be watching closely in their Week 6 matchup versus the defending Super Bowl champions. Can the Broncos find a […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos leaves the field after his team defeated the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos host the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football . Earlier today, I discussed how the Broncos can earn their fourth win of the season. Now, I’ll turn my focus to three major storylines I’ll be watching closely in their Week 6 matchup versus the defending Super Bowl champions. Can the Broncos find a weakness in the Seahawks defense? Five weeks into the 2026 season and the Broncos are still a mess on offense. Denver was able to escape Los Angeles with a victory, yet that was mostly due to an incredible fourth quarter effort by the defense. Yes, the offense was able to capitalize on short fields, but their drive-to-drive consistency was an absolute trainwreck. All of Broncos Country hopes the offense can find a way to get back on track. Unfortunately, their Week 6 opponent sports one of the best defenses in the National Football League. I’m having a tough time finding a weakness for Denver to exploit, but they’ll have to find one to be victorious in primetime. The Seahawks are fantastic across the board defensively. They have a knack forcing turnovers with 11 on the season. They are third best in the league on third down allowing less than 30-percent conversion rate. That’s an area the Broncos have struggled with all year long—exemplified by their dreadful 1-of-12 in that respect against the Chargers. The Seahawks are giving up roughly 150 yards on the air. Given such, teams have run the ball at a high rate against them. Alas, it’s tough to establish a formidable ground attack against them. They are allowing 100 yards per game, but barely over 3.5 yards per carry. Head Coach Sean Payton emphasized the importance of being able to run the ball to take pressure of Bo Nix and set him up for success. I have a feeling they will try to do that against Seattle. But can they grind hard enough on the ground to find a way to win? We will see of Denver’s offensive line and running backs are up to the challenge. Will Bo Nix finally get out of his third-year slump? One of my key points for victory earlier today was Bo Nix letting it rip . That’s a big ask of the third-year signal caller who will be one of the league’s premier passing defenses. However, the time is running out for excuses. I’m not asking for a huge game from Nix. The odds of that happening are slim and none. As noted, the Seahawks are stopping opposing aerial attacks from launching on a weekly basis. But we have to see starting caliber play from Nix. How he is performing right now just doesn’t meet the mark. I want to see him be decisive in the pocket. He also needs to use his legs help move the chains. I want to see some aggressiveness with down the field throws. Just because the Seahawks are good against the pass doesn’t mean he has to be hesitant to try and make a big play. Quarterbacks need splash plays to help their team win. There are opportunities being missed every game because he isn’t pulling the trigger or letting plays develop. For whatever reason, Nix seems way too cautious out there. Has he lost his moxie and confidence? Your mileage may vary, but it sure seems like it. Can he find a way to get them back on Thursday Night Football ? How will Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph combat the Seahawks’ one-dimensional offense? The Seahawks boast a Top 10 scoring offense. That comes as a mild surprise, especially with their ground game being an issue. In fact, that might be their biggest weakness as a team. Zach Charbonnet is still recovering from injury and is yet to play this season. He’s trying his best to get ready to play, but Mike Macdonald said it’s highly unlikely Charbonnet will be able to go. Additionally, Rookie Jadarian Price is on injured reserve. That means Emanuel Wilson and George Holani are poised to get majority of the carries on Thursday Night Football . Neither are performing well—barely averaging over 3 yards per carry. I’d say that’s part of the reason Sam Darnold has looked a bit erratic coming back from his early Week 1 injury. Truth be told, the Seahawks have been a one-man show on offense. Fourth-year wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba has been electric. The reining Offensive Player of the Year accounts for a third of their passing offense’s targets with a staggering 50 on the season. Overall, he basically has half of their passing yardage and touchdown output. I’m thinking Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph is going to opt to have an extra man over the top to limit Smith-Njigba’s big play ability. We already know the Broncos will be without Patrick Surtain II and they may be without Riley Moss for another week in addition to safety Talanoa Hufagna. Denver’s pass rush was able to rattle the Chargers’ banged up offensive line and limit Justin Herbert, who was without his top three receivers last Sunday. Thursday’s primetime matchup will be the complete opposite. In addition to Smith-Njigba, Joseph and his players will need to account for Rashid Shaheed and Cooper Kupp. Shaheed has great speed and is a deep threat that will challenge the Broncos secondary. And while he may not be the player he once was, Kupp is still extremely efficient moving the chains when targeted. I’ll be keeping a close eye on how Denver’s hampered secondary performs against the Seahawks’ passing attack.
author: Christopher Hart

title: How the Denver Broncos can beat the Seattle Seahawks
summary: The Denver Broncos host the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football. The Broncos are coming off a close victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. Meanwhile, the Seahawks are looking to rebound after losing a nailbiter to the San Francisco 49ers. In order to topple the Seahawks in primetime, here are three […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Inglewood, California, USA; Denver Broncos safety Brandon Jones (22) celebrates an interception against the Los Angeles Chargers during the second half at SoFi Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gary A. Vasquez-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Denver Broncos host the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football . The Broncos are coming off a close victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. Meanwhile, the Seahawks are looking to rebound after losing a nailbiter to the San Francisco 49ers. In order to topple the Seahawks in primetime, here are three things the Broncos have to accomplish. No more excuses: It’s time for Bo Nix to rip it and deliver through the air There is no doubt the offense has drastically taken a step back five games into their 2026 gridiron campaign. Broncos Country is no stranger to slow starts in this respect. However, what we have seen thus far is easily the worst during the Sean Payton era. Without question, there is a lot of blame to go around. But let’s be brutally honest—quarterback Bo Nix is not playing well at all. There has been no third-year jump from the former first-round pick. In fact, it’s been an abysmal third year slump. All things considered, the Broncos are quite lucky to be 3-2 given his poor play to date. After their victory over the Chargers, Head Coach Sean Payton expressed confidence with Nix and hopes to see him ‘rip it’ in the weeks to come. But here is the kicker, the Seahawks have one of the best defenses in the NFL. They’ve already forced 11 turnovers on the season. Moreover, they haven’t let an opposing quarterback throw for more than 200 yards on them thus far. This is arguably the toughest matchup for Nix and the offense yet. Seattle has an elite pass defense . Regardless, that can’t be an excuse for poor play. He needs to step up in the pocket and deliver throws. No more bailing out of clean pockets when there is good enough protection. It’s time for him to start figuring things out. Star wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba’s impact has to be kept to a minimum First things first. I came away impressed with how Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine performed against the Chargers. Los Angeles was missing their top trio of receivers which can’t be ignored. Even so, I felt the two cornerbacks performed admirably with Denver’s top boundary duo of Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss sidelined. Even so, this is one matchup Broncos Country will wish they had Surtain in the starting lineup. Why? Because Jaxon Smith-Njigba is one of the best receivers in the NFL—a premier playmaker who can do it all. Smith-Njigba is coming off an incredible 2025 campaign. His performance and production were elite. The fourth-year pro led the NFL with 1,793 receiving yards on 119 catches with 10 touchdowns. That was good enough to earn him first-team All-Pro honors, his second Pro-Bowl accolade, as well as the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year award. It’s not going to be easy, but Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph has to come up with a game plan that limits the star wide receiver’s impact on the game. That will be quite the challenge with a banged-up secondary that will likely be without star safety Talanoa Hufanga who suffered an ankle injury late in the game versus the Chargers. Razor thin margins: The Broncos have to win the turnover battle One of the best developments for the Broncos this season is their defense being able to take the ball away from opponents. They have forced seven turnovers on defense through five games. In addition, they’ve came up in the clutch along with several additional fourth down stops. In order to secure a primetime victory on Thursday Night Football , the Broncos will need their defense to continue doing that. Winning the turnover battle, especially with Seattle’s defense being elite at forcing them, is an absolute must. The past three games, quarterback Sam Darnold has made his fair share of plays through the air. Though he has also made a lot of boneheaded mistakes with five interceptions during that time span. Denver’s pass rush came alive late in the game against the Chargers, but it’s important to keep in mind they were starting four rookies in their offensive trenches. Seattle’s offensive line isn’t perfect, but it’s a lot better than what Denver faced on Sunday. Putting pressure on Darnold to force him to make some mistakes will be huge. Hopefully, the Broncos’ defensive front seven can keep their momentum going and come up with a few big plays that help turn the tide in Denver’s favor in primetime.
author: Christopher Hart

title: Broncos at Chargers: The No Bull Review
summary: In the NFL, a win is a win. I’m sure many of you out there in Broncos Country felt like I did for much of this game: Frustrated. The offense looks largely broken and disjointed. The defense swings between elite and derptastic. Props to the Los Angeles Chargers. They were missing something close to half […]
full_text: In the NFL, a win is a win. I’m sure many of you out there in Broncos Country felt like I did for much of this game: Frustrated. The offense looks largely broken and disjointed. The defense swings between elite and derptastic. Props to the Los Angeles Chargers. They were missing something close to half of their starters coming into this game and gave the Denver Broncos one hell of a fight. Offense I don’t for one second think that changing play callers had any serious impact on the play of the offense overall. The problem with the offense is about execution and the players, not about scheme and play calling. Hopefully Davis Webb feels a bit vindicated that Payton took over play calling only to have the offense look hapless against a winless team. The one serious nit to pick has to do with the clock and play management at the end of the 4th quarter. They could have gotten a play in and ran it at the last second, but wasted a timeout instead. They then took a delay of game immediately. I can not begin to understand how that happens. It was ineptitude of the highest order and lands directly at the feet of Sean Payton. While many players had many gaffes that cost the team in several ways, you can rest assured the play caller cost us an opportunity to put the game away during that series. Quarterbacks Whatever we did with Bo Nix heading into this season needs to be largely thrown in the trash and never repeated in upcoming years. Nix still looks out of sync, rushed, and inaccurate through 5 games so far this year. We saw this same level of play last season, but it appears that we’re stuck in a Groundhog Day loop with our quarterback development. I think next offseason Nix better be playing quite a few more snaps in the preseason in order to knock the rust off and hit the ground running. I’m pretty curious about why Nix audibled into a run play on 3rd and 9. There’s no real way for us to know this, but it seemed like a give-up play to me. Yes, the Chargers’ defense is good. But there just seemed to be no gusto whatsoever for attacking throughout the game, and this was but one example of that. In the past two years, Nix has been one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL at avoiding sacks, yet in this game he sacked himself running right into the left side of the pocket. He also was getting tackled and gave up a fumble, one-arming the ball. I’d complain more, but across the field from him was a quarterback who did an even worse job in this game of protecting the ball. On the positive side (that just adds to the frustration), he showed off his arm on a big pass outside to Waddle as he was getting hit in the knees. He drilled a couple of outs to the sideline that were nice throws to both Humphreys and Sutton. His touchdown throw was quickly delivered and on point. Much like the game overall, we saw a frustrating amount of bad quarterbacking in this game along with a sprinkle of good play. Line Hats off to the line for some exceptional blocking outside on the first touchdown by Dobbins, with Sutton, Bolles, and Powers all leading the way to an easy score in the run game. But honestly, the line is not blocking up the run game early, and it is a big part of the problem with our offense. The pattern still holds that this line doesn’t really open up lanes until late in the game. This points to excellent conditioning for our linemen, as they really did start winning at the line of scrimmage in the 4th quarter. They have to figure out how to win in the trenches earlier. Their pass blocking was spotty this game. Part of that has to do with the Chargers’ front, but I’m not sure how well we can expect Nix to stay in the pocket more when it’s collapsing from one side on a good number of pass plays (especially 3rd downs, which was one reason they did so poorly in that area this week). Running Backs JK Dobbins got force-fed the ball this week. He started off quite slow with runs of 2, 0, 1, 2(TD), 1, 6, 5, 4, 0, 3, 0, and 3 through 3 quarters for an average of a little more than 2 yards per carry. Of course, once the 4th quarter gets here, Dobbins wakes up and has runs of 3, 14, 1, 13, 2, 4, 7. Sure, the average at the end of the game looks decent. But this back is not playing well enough. Last year he would bounce out of tackles and create a couple extra yards. This year he is looking pretty pedestrian regularly. Giving him so many ineffective carries early does not serve the offense. Did you know that RJ Harvey was on the field for 23 snaps? I wouldn’t have guessed since we didn’t see much of him. He was run up the middle a couple of times for practically nothing and only had one catch for 0 yards in the passing game. I’m not sure how a guy who is such an explosive player isn’t being used more to help kick-start the offense. I do know they had him in pass blocking on a 3rd down that went poorly. He’s not the back that can slow down a linebacker (that would be Badie). Receivers Evan Engram had himself a game against the Chargers with 4 catches on 4 targets for 55 yards to lead the team. He had a big time catch on one of the best executed plays we’ve seen from the Broncos in a couple of weeks. Jaylen Waddle’s best play this game was a nice end around for 8 yards. For what seems like the 3rd week in a row, he dropped another pass that hit his hands (though it was a very poor throw by Nix, I expect highly paid WRs to catch it if it hits their hands). Cortland Sutton continues to look largely washed as our #1 WR. He shoved a defender to get an offensive pass interference call. He dropped a makeable jump ball on 3rd down. He finally caught a 13-yard pass left open on the sideline. He did get a gimme touchdown on a completely busted coverage by the defensive back lined up across from him. Defense I don’t think anyone out there in Broncos Country thoroughly enjoyed the defensive performance in this game. There were several plays that had more of the poor tackling issues we saw earlier in the year. That being said, the defense was the #1 reason the Broncos won this game. They got pressure on Herbert. They forced 3 fumbles. They got an interception as well. They also made a 4th-and-1 stop to effectively turn the ball over. Sure, Herbert had a couple of nice runs. One of them was a perfectly executed play and superb scheme from McDonald to get Herbert a free lane to the sideline for a gain of 23 yards. The only guy I could see Vance Joseph using as a spy on Herbert would be Srnad, and he’s too valuable in coverage to do that. Front 7 Nik Bonitto finally had a breakout game this week. He had two big sacks on 3rd down, 3 tackles for loss, and 2 quarterback hits. Zach Allen again had a big impact on the field. He had a sack, a tackle for loss, a quarterback hit, and forced one of the defense’s three fumbles. DJ Jones had his best game of the season against the Chargers. He was wrecking the Chargers from the interior with 1 sack, 1 tackle for loss, 1 quarterback hit, and a forced fumble. Jonah Elliss also flashed some plays from what I saw. He had two nice pass rushes forcing throwaways. Neither play will show up on the stat sheet, but they were big plus plays in my books. Alex Singleton laid down the hammer at the line of scrimmage with a thundering hit early for a gain of 0. Singleton made an absolutely embarrassing attempt at a tackle on 3rd and 15, giving up a first down that he should have stopped. He had a great nose for the ball on a tackle for loss on an outside toss play. He whiffs on the next play, giving up a big gain on a pass to the outside. Justin Strnad made a nice TFL attacking the edge on an outside run. Nice tackle in the last drive in a one-on-one coverage situation. He also earned a pass defense, slapping the ball out at the last second on an out route. Que Robinson definitely deserves a shout-out for stopping Herbert on a sneak on 4th and 1. It was a key play of the game by the young outside linebacker. Secondary This week it was Brandon Jones’ turn to be a star…
author: sadaraine

title: Broncos’ stats and analysis vs. Chargers
summary: By most accounts the Denver Broncos should have won this game in a blowout, and yet, this team managed to need another fourth quarter comeback from Bo Nix to get a win after being down 17-10 in the fourth quarter. The Los Angeles Chargers were starting an offensive line with almost no experience and they […]
full_text: By most accounts the Denver Broncos should have won this game in a blowout, and yet, this team managed to need another fourth quarter comeback from Bo Nix to get a win after being down 17-10 in the fourth quarter. The Los Angeles Chargers were starting an offensive line with almost no experience and they were missing their best WR on offense in Ladd McConkey. The Charger starting offensive line was Jake Slaughter, Travis Burke, Alex Harkey, Logan Taylor, and Cole Strange. Harkey had never taken an NFL snap on offense. Slaughter is a rookie who has started all five games so far. Burke and Taylor are both rookies who were making their first career starts. Strange is a journeyman veteran on his fourth team in five NFL seasons, but he did enter the game with 48 starts. This OL was facing the defense that led the NFL in sacks in both 2024 and 2025. The Bronco defense should have been making life miserable for Justin Herbert, but that didn’t really happen in the fourth quarter. The Bronco defense did have five sacks and six QBhits (remember a hit is not sack, and a sack is not a QBhit), but all but one of those happened in the fourth quarter. The one that didn’t was Nik Bonitto’s sack on the last play of the first quarter. Nik had a great game on paper with 3 TFL, 2 QBhits, 2 sacks, and 4 tackles (3 solo), but he didn’t seem to have that big of an influence on the game and he really should have dominated against a team starting two backup OTs. Three TFL is a career high for him. His season high was 16 in 2024. While he got 3 in this game, he only has four on the season. The Bronco defense gave up another long run. This time was similar to the others in that the opposing RB broke a bunch of tackles on route to the endzone. The Bronco defense joins the Colts and the Raiders as the only defenses who have allowed three runs of 30+ this season. Those would be the 30 yard run by Kyren Williams, the 42 yard TD run by Kimani Vidal Sassoon, and the 60 yard TD run by Kenneth Walker. At the time of writing, prior to the Monday night game, the Bronco run defense is 25th in YPC allowed at 4.7. The Jaguars are the best allowing 2.9 and the Panthers are the worst at 5.4. What’s more troubling is the third down conversion percentage allowed. The Broncos were one of the best teams in the league over the last two seasons at stopping conversion on 3rd down. They currently stand at 26th – allowing conversion on 45.2 percent. The Cowboys are the worst at 52.6 percent and the Vikings are the best at 22.2 percent (this helps explain their 5-0 start). The Denver defense has allowed 33 third down conversions so far this season. Only the Lions have allowed more at 36. The Bears have allowed 13. Will Lutz was extremely reliable last season even hitting 4 of 6 from 50 or longer. He is currently 3 of 6 from 40 or longer with two of those misses coming from 40-49 yards. Currently NFL kickers are 75 for 91 from that distance (81.5 percent). Lutz only missed two from that distance all last year and he now has two misses from that range. While Lutz has been having a bad season so far, Jeremy Crawshaw has been having a great season. He has gotten 50 percent of his punts downed inside the 20 (12 of 24), and 8 of 24 have been downed inside the 10. Using my system that rewards punts downed inside the 10 with increasingly more value as you get to the one, Crawshaw is currently 5th with 34 points. A punt downed at the 10 gets one point, while a punt downed at the 1 gets 10 points. Notice how the Bengal’s punter has five downed inside the ten, but four of them were downed at the 8. He only gets 14 points, while the Steeler’s punter, who also has five, has 35 points, because he has one downed at the four, one at the two, and one at the one. Every team has at least one, but the Viking punter only has one and it was downed at the 10. This stat is a punter stat, but it is also a punt coverage team stat. The Bronco punt coverage team has been really good so far this year. I don’t know how many of Crawshaw’s inside the 10 punts were “coffin corner” punts where he angled them out of bounds. I know he is good at that and has done it as least four times this season that I can remember. Only six on Crawshaw’s 24 punts have been returned and those are only averaging 7.7 yards per return. That’s currently tied for the second least YPR in the NFL. Only the Packers punt coverage team has been better (7.4 yards per PR). 25 percent return rate is one of the lowest in the NFL. Michael Dickson of the Seahawks has the lowest at 15 percent, while Rigoberto Sanchez of the Colts has had 69 percent of his returned.
author: Joe Mahoney

title: Denver Broncos news: ‘Finding a way to win’ is still winning, no matter how ugly
summary: Following an ugly but effective 23-17 win over the Chargers on Sunday, quarterback Bo Nix was the first to admit it wasn’t “his best.” “The game, the feel and the results of drives told me that it wasn’t necessarily pretty, but we just found a way to win,” Nix said, adding the offense as a […]
full_text: Following an ugly but effective 23-17 win over the Chargers on Sunday, quarterback Bo Nix was the first to admit it wasn’t “his best.” “The game, the feel and the results of drives told me that it wasn’t necessarily pretty, but we just found a way to win,” Nix said, adding the offense as a whole was OK. “At the end of the day, we’ve got to score more points, and that’s something that we’re going to continue to work on.” The problem, as Nix sees it, is consistency. “Right now, there’s just a little subtle piece of overall offensive execution that we’re still working towards, because at times, it’s there and we’re really good,” he said. “At times, for whatever reason, the drive stalls.” “I don’t think we win the game without those turnovers,” Nix said, noting the offense should have been able to get touchdowns instead of field goals out of the short fields. So we need to clean that up.” Bo NIX If it weren’t for the defense, which practically gift-wrapped 13 points for the offense, it would have been a much messier day and not a win. “I don’t think we win the game without those turnovers,” Nix said, noting the offense should have been able to get touchdowns out of those short fields instead of having to settle for field goals. “So we need to clean that up.” Head coach Sean Payton thinks a big part of the answer is better protection up front. “I think it’s important from a protection standpoint, that early in games we provide that clean pocket so that clock doesn’t get juiced up a little bit,” Payton added. Of course, Nix’s footwork bears some responsibility for the offense’s struggles too. Payton thinks the QB is “settling down a little bit,” but the coach reiterated his complaint from last week that the entire team, especially the offense, needs to be good at the details. “I think after four weeks there’s a handful of things that collectively — and you know, it starts with me — where it’s like, all right, let’s focus on these details,” Payton said. “And I think the byproduct helps the [quarterback].” “[Bo Nix]'s really, really, right now, struggling with just his feet in the pocket.” @danorlovsky7 breaks down what's going wrong for the Broncos' QB recently 😬 (Via @PatMcAfeeShow ) pic.twitter.com/SNpUUl0A0q — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) October 12, 2026 No matter Nix’s struggles this season, Payton has let him know he’s guy the coach wants in control. “I said to him ‘man, you’re the guy we want here. Let’s go. You’ve done a ton of things well.’ But I think a lot goes into that,” Payton noted. “I want him to make sure that we can let it rip.” For Nix that means trusting what he sees. “You’ve got to sort of earn that right,” Nix added. “When you do the preparation, you earn the right to react so that you can let it rip.” The main problem with that is Nix and the offense “earn the right” one series and then lose it the next. “I’ll say it again, you’re always looking for small steps [of improvement.] Sean Payton “There were times I felt like I was really good when the play was there,” Nix said. “There’s other times I feel like there’s still some things that I could either see or process better. …It’s just the layers and layers of being a quarterback and processing. Nothing’s ever going to be easy,” Payton reiterated that he coaches for small steps of improvement — and as coach he’s accountable for that too — particularly when it comes to calling protections so the offense can convert a few more (or any!) third downs. “I’ll say it again, you’re always looking for small steps,” Payton added. “The strength of that front, the edges can be a problem, and then they do a pretty good job with some zone pressures.” Nix joked it would be great if the defense lined up exactly like they wanted because “you’d probably have a lot of touchdowns and a lot of points.” But that’s not going to happen. “The important thing is we’re sitting here talking about a win,” Nix added. “That’s really, really important.”

title: Checking in on former Detroit Lions players lost this offseason
summary: This offseason, the Detroit Lions made an unusual amount of changes to their roster. With a tightening salary cap and a need to get younger, the Lions said goodbye to several players who had long been part of the organizaiton. With the Lions on their bye week, we thought this would be a good chance […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 08: Alex Anzalone #34 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers reacts following an interception during a game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on October 08, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images This offseason, the Detroit Lions made an unusual amount of changes to their roster. With a tightening salary cap and a need to get younger, the Lions said goodbye to several players who had long been part of the organizaiton. With the Lions on their bye week, we thought this would be a good chance to check in on those departed players and see how they’re doing with their new teams. RB David Montgomery New team: Texans Stats: 52 carries, 138 yards (2.7 YPC), 2 TDs; 7 catches, 67 yards, 1 TD PFF grade: 68.1 (20th out of 53) Montgomery is getting a bigger share of carries than he would’ve in Detroit (Woody Marks has 11 more carries than Montgomery at 149), but the efficiency numbers have fallen off a cliff. Montgomery’s 2.7 yards per carry is the lowest of his career by a full yard, and his 40.4% rushing success rate is also a career-low. Unfortunately, Montgomery suffered a groin injury last week, and is considered week-to-week. WR Kalif Raymond New team: Bears Stats: 24 catches, 226 yards, 1 TD; 9 punt returns, 93 yards (10.3 avg.) PFF grade: 73.0 (34th out of 97) Raymond is already close to surpassing his yardage total from last year with the Lions (289) and is on pace for a career year. He has played in 62.4% of the Bears’ offensive snaps, which is his highest percentage since his first year in Detroit (71.4%). But his production has slowed down, catching five passes for 12 total yards in the last two games combined—albeit with a pair of backup quarterbacks. WR Greg Dortch New team: Bills Stats: 0 catches; 9 punt returns, 84 yards (9.3 avg.); 16 kick returns, 421 yards (26.3 avg.) PFF grade: 72.1 return grade (12th out of 70th) Dortch has only played in 11 snaps on offense, but he’s been a solid returner for the Bills—something the Lions could certainly use after the injury to Tom Kennedy. Dortch’s punt return average is below league average, but his kick return average is just above it. G Kayode Awosika New team: Chargers Stats: 2 starts PFF grade: 59.2 (44th out of 81) Awosika won the starting left guard job for the Chargers out of training camp, but has missed the last three games with a fibula injury. For what it’s worth, he’s currently graded higher than Lions’ reserve guard Ben Bartch (48.0). DT Roy Lopez New team: Cardinals Stats: 5 starts — 20 tackles, 1.0 sacks, 3 TFLs PFF grade: 71.3 (21st out of 140) As Lions fans saw a taste of on Sunday, Lopez continues to play strong football on the interior. He’s been a big reason why the Cardinals have a strong run defense, and he flashed some of his pass rushing chops with his first sack of the season opposite Juice Scruggs. DT DJ Reader New team: Giants Stats: 5 starts—13 tackles PFF grade: 85.8 (2nd out of 140) Reader apparently still has it at age 32. He’s not only continued to be a strong run defender (77.4, fourth), but PFF is giving him an outstanding pass rushing grade at 78.5 (eighth) despite only producing five pressures this year. Also interesting, despite having Reader playing at his best, the Giants run defense is giving up the second-highest yards per carry average (5.2) in the NFL. EDGE Al-Quadin Muhammad New team: Buccaneers Stats: 5 games, 2 starts — 4 tackles, 2 QB hits, 0.0 sacks PFF grade: 77.1 (24th out of 123) Muhammad’s standard stat sheet is quite bear, as he continues to look for his first sack of the season and only has four pressures through five games. However, PFF credits him with above average scores in every phase of the game. EDGE Marcus Davenport New team: Bears (now retired) Stats: 1 game — 1 tackle PFF grade: 70.8 I felt compelled to add Davenport to this list, given he was considered a starter in Detroit. He made the Bears’ practice squad, got an elevation for a game, and announced his retirement from football last week. EDGE Tyrus Wheat New team: Cowboys Stats: 4 games — 3 tackles (14 defensive snaps, 67 special teams snaps) PFF grade: 61.9 PFF special teams grade After logging 215 special teams snaps for the Lions last year, Wheat remains a staple on the third phase of the game in Dallas. LB Alex Anzalone New team: Buccaneers Stats: 5 starts — 27 tackles, 1.0 sacks, 1 INT PFF grade: 41.1 (75 out of 76) Anzalone’s start to his Tampa career was a complete disaster, with fans calling for his benching after just two games. He’s since settled in a bit, and he helped the Bucs get their first win of the season on Thursday with a game-clinching interception. What has been particularly concerning about his play is missed tackles. He had four in the first two games of the season after tallying just eight all of last year. LB Grant Stuard New team: Rams Stats: 5 games — 2 tackles (0 defensive snaps, 99 special teams snaps) PFF grade: 66.9 special teams grade Stuard remains a four-core special teamer with the Rams, but has yet to find the field on defense. CB Amik Robertson New team: Commanders Stats: 5 starts — 33 tackles, 8 passes defended, 1 forced fumble PFF grade: 74.9 (13th out of 111) If there’s one player the Lions may regret letting go, it’s Robertson—who signed a lucrative two-year, $15 million contract with Washington this offseason. Robertson has been excellent, leading the league with eight passes defended. He’s allowed a passer rating of just 79.8 when targeted (17 catches on 31 targets for 158 yards and 1 TD). However, he does have five penalties on the season—second-most among all cornerbacks. And he remains an elite run defender—producing an 87.3 grade in that phase, fifth-best among all cornerbacks. S Daniel Thomas New team: Browns Stats: 3 games (0 starts) — 4 tackles (0 defensive snaps, 64 special teams snaps) PFF grade: 69.8 special teams grade The Lions didn’t have room for Thomas after overhauling the safety room, but he’s been an effective special teamer in Cleveland Notable former Lions with no playing time QB Kyle Allen (Bills) TE Shane Zylstra (unsigned) C Graham Glasgow (unsigned) OT Taylor Decker (unsigned) EDGE Josh Paschal (unsigned) LB Zach Cunningham (unsigned)
