title: Detroit Lions WR Jameson Williams gets celebration fine rescinded
summary: A few weeks ago, the Detroit Lions were hammered by the NFL with a load of fines for celebrations. In their Week 2 loss to the Buffalo Bills, several Lions players mimicked a smoking motion—resulting in the following fines: On Tuesday, it was revealed that Williams appealed his two fines and won both of those […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Jameson Williams #1 of the Detroit Lions looks on prior to the game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images A few weeks ago, the Detroit Lions were hammered by the NFL with a load of fines for celebrations. In their Week 2 loss to the Buffalo Bills, several Lions players mimicked a smoking motion—resulting in the following fines: Amon-Ra St. Brown: $14,926 — Illegal celebration and vulgar acts Amon-Ra St. Brown: $14,926 — Illegal celebration and vulgar acts Amon-Ra St. Brown: $14,926 — Illegal celebration and vulgar acts Amon-Ra St. Brown: $14,926 — Illegal celebration and vulgar acts Penei Sewell: $14,926 — Illegal celebration and vulgar acts Jahmyr Gibbs: $14,926 — Illegal celebartion and vulgar acts Jameson Williams: $14,926 — Illegal celebration and vulgar acts Jameson Williams: $11,941 — Taunting On Tuesday, it was revealed that Williams appealed his two fines and won both of those appeals. According to Ian Rapoport, Williams argued that marijuana was legal in several states and therefore not an obscene gesture. As for the taunting penalty, the brief gesture he made, Williams argued, was not offensive. At this point, it isn’t clear if any of the other Lions players won their appeals, but St. Brown told reporters the in Week 3 that he was planning on appealing with the league. Appeals officer—and Hall of Fame linebacker—Derrick Brooks offered the following response to Williams’ appeal. “Although I rescinded this fine, please make every effort to celebrate with your teammates in the best professional manner possible.” This offseason, the NFL attempted to cut down on celebrations that referenced drugs or alcohol. In the same week the Lions got hit, players like 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk and Cowboys tight end Jake Ferguson were fined for their “chugging” celebrations. Since then, both of their fines have also been rescinded.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Where do the Detroit Lions go from here?
summary: Through five games, the Detroit Lions are 3-2. With a stuttering offense akin to an engine during a Michigan winter, and a defense more uneven than Chris Ilitch’s commitment to the city of Detroit, where does this team go from here? Monday’s reactions to the Lions victory over the Arizona Cardinals, 45-21, seemed to track […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions scores a three-yard rushing touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals during the NFL game at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. The Lions defeated the Cardinals 45-21. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through five games, the Detroit Lions are 3-2. With a stuttering offense akin to an engine during a Michigan winter, and a defense more uneven than Chris Ilitch’s commitment to the city of Detroit, where does this team go from here? Monday’s reactions to the Lions victory over the Arizona Cardinals, 45-21, seemed to track for a portion of the fan base that had already grabbed their pitchforks. The slow start had them marching due west to continue the call for Kelvin Sheppard after Jacoby Brissett marched 73 yards in 14 plays for a touchdown. A second straight three-and-out for the offense… and then a third one to cap off Detroit’s performance in the first quarter had me wondering if any of us were getting out of this alive. A bye week to stew over a performance like this would have been enough for me to put in my two weeks at Pride of Detroit. But, eventually, that engine turned over, and the offense started humming more reliably than your father’s favorite automobile. An entire quarter of nothing—less than nothing—against the Cardinals led to 31 unanswered points on five consecutive drives. In the meantime, the defense forced five straight three-and-outs of their own from Arizona. Prior to Sunday, the Lions defense had only forced a total of five three-and-outs—tied for the fewest with Kansas City and Jacksonville. Detroit hadn’t played such perfectly complementary football since who knows how long. Pay Sam LaPorta Sam LaPorta needs to get paid, so Brad Holmes and all the cap people might find themselves on a much more working vacation this week than they had planned. LaPorta, henceforth known as the guy who will not have the health of his back questioned after Mack Wilson launched into him like a T-1000, is the kind of talent Detroit so desperately missed down the stretch last season. It’s ultra clear how important he is to this offense. At this point, his contributions this season have been more palpable than any other offensive playmaker not named Jahmyr Gibbs. He’s first in contested catch rate (83.3%) among pass catchers with at least two contested targets, and second in yards after catch per reception (5.3) of anyone with more than 17 targets through five weeks. He’s second in yards per reception (11.7) behind only Jameson Williams (15.3) for any receiver with at least 10 catches. Among the four key playmakers for Detroit, LaPorta is very clearly the second-best option behind a player who just broke Barry Sanders’ NFL record for touchdowns scored by a player before turning 25. Pay him; pay that man his money. The Curious Case of Amon-Ra St. Brown St. Brown’s rather pedestrian start to the 2026 season is proof the receiver is human. In a game where he fumbled the ball twice—lucky enough to have special teams ace Tay Martin and Tate Ratledge recover both of them—and dropped at least one pass we’ve seen him catch routinely, the Lions scored 45 points in less than three quarters of football. He’s one of the best receivers in football, off to a bit of a slow start by his standards, but think of what that means for this Lions offense. It’s truly too talented to accept mediocrity, as suggested by Dan Campbell, and it’s too multifaceted to fail. Keith Abney? The fifth-round rookie cornerback? Campbell and Sheppard both talked about shuffling the personnel ahead of their Week 5 matchup with Arizona, but who knew it meant taking a fifth-round rookie pegged to be a slot cornerback and playing him at deep safety? Abney was one of the most valuable selections in the entire 2026 NFL Draft according to consensus boards , but with only 25 defensive snaps in the slot Week 1, and some inactive designations sprinkled in between here and now, that’s a pretty bold move to have him play 59 of the team’s 73 snaps on defense. “I thought he was solid,” Campbell said about Abney’s performance on Sunday. “The things that popped up for him were the ‘hey, I haven’t done this before,’ which is what you want for a rookie […] I thought he played a good game, you know? First start—first NFL start—at safety, never played safety. He’s banked some reps for us, you know, we’ve been cross-training him. But man, there’s meat on the bone there, and he’s got room to grow, and we feel like he can continue to grow and get better.” Can you feel that? Brian Branch returning just in time to pair with Abney, who the Lions see as a young player with potential to grow and improve? Do you know what that is? It’s the Lions secondary slowly putting itself back together because contrary to popular belief, Humpty Dumpty can’t hurt you. Lots of things like quicksand and black holes and Humpty Dumpty end up playing a much lesser role in your life than you would have anticipated at age 9. You’re taking Jahmyr Gibbs for granted You just are. Maybe you think you’re appreciating what Gibbs is doing week in and week out, but you’re not. Does the name Kerryon Johnson mean anything to you? Years, plural—five of them, to be exact—the Lions went without a single player rushing for 100 yards, and now you have Gibbs breaking records each and every week. Gibbs is so good— “How good is he?”— Gibbs is so good each week, we’re highlighting the performances of other players on offense before Gibbs because the old adage is true, you save the best for last. Look at our website: not a single writer chose to use an image of Gibbs as their featured image for their article. Hell, I’m guilty of it myself by starting this article talking about Sam LaPorta, mostly so his day doesn’t pale in comparison to a guy who gained 207 all-purpose yards and scored two touchdowns. And another thing, Jared Goff is having a darn good season. Any time you can start your season with 12 touchdowns to 0 interceptions, you’re doing great. He’s certainly doing a lot more than “for sure not helping” out the offense , but there’s very clearly a rank and file for MVP candidates on this offense—and Gibbs is at the head of the table. It’s not a slight to Goff, it’s just so boring and tired and frankly uninspiring to say that the QB with the best numbers on a team headed for the playoffs should be the first choice for the league’s most valuable player. Watch a Lions game and tell me which player this offense couldn’t bear to be without. Hint: it’s the one everyone keeps handwringing over his usage for fear his body can’t withstand the punishment of a 17-game NFL season. So where are the Lions headed from here? A win over the Cardinals, no matter how convincing it was, wasn’t going to do too much for the fans who had already made up their minds on the defense. And with the slow start on offense, there’s another talking point for those skeptical of the Lions chances to be a true contender. But this team, despite a slightly disappointing 3-2 start, is getting reinforcements on the other side of their early-season bye. Branch, if healthy, is a bona fide difference maker. Cade Mays will be an upgrade at the center position, not only raising the ceiling of the offensive line, but also further fortifying the depth should they need to call on Juice Scruggs in the future. They’re not the brand new additions fans have called for after the first four games, especially on the defensive side of the ball, but that won’t make them any less impactful. The lesson to be learned from this rollercoaster ride to start the season is this league is full of weird. The Los Angeles Rams have a worse record than the Cleveland Browns, Las Vegas Raiders, and New York Giants through five weeks. The transitive property does not compute in the NFL. It’s a long season, but Lions are still headed for the playoffs in a mucked up NFC.
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Week 6 power rankings: Lions enter their bye week just outside Top 10
summary: The Detroit Lions (3-2) enter their Week 6 bye after a 45-21 win over the Arizona Cardinals, hoping they can make the right defensive adjustments to stay competitive for the rest of the season. The Lions offense has done a lot of the heavy lifting to get them to a winning record, and they currently […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell takes the field for during the first half against Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (3-2) enter their Week 6 bye after a 45-21 win over the Arizona Cardinals, hoping they can make the right defensive adjustments to stay competitive for the rest of the season. The Lions offense has done a lot of the heavy lifting to get them to a winning record, and they currently sit in the Top 5 rankings in several categories, including points per game (32.8, T-1st), EPA per play (+0.13, 4th), and touchdowns scored (20, T-1st), amongst others. Their offense gives them a chance to win any given week, and their defense is taking steps forward, but is that enough to sway the national narrative? Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings. NFL.com: 11 (Previous rank: 16) From Nick Shook : The Lions wiped the floor with the Cardinals over the final three quarters of Sunday’s lopsided victory. Jared Goff distributed the ball among his many talented pass catchers, torching Arizona’s undisciplined defense for 271 yards and three touchdowns. Most importantly, Detroit’s defense finally showed up! We’ll see if the latter holds with star safety Brian Branch nearing his return. ESPN: 11 (Previous rank: 16) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Biggest issue on defense: A depleted secondary Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard was under fire after Detroit gave up 30 points in three of its first four games, though the Lions enjoyed a much better performance Sunday before heading into their bye week. The biggest struggles have been in the secondary, as they’ve given up a league-high 1,487 passing yards. To Detroit’s defense, they entered the season without Pro Bowl safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph. And they’re are missing safety Thomas Harper and defensive back Avonte Maddox, who are on injured reserve. Branch should return for Week 7 after being sidelined since December because of a torn Achilles. Sports Illustrated: 11 ( Previous rank: 18) From Connor Orr : Brian Branch’s anticipated return looms as the Lions hit a bye week after throttling the Cardinals. There are worse ways to enter your break. While I am backing off my prediction that this team will win 14 games, I don’t think winning the division is off the table by any stretch. The Athletic: 12 (Previous rank: 12) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : Sunday: Beat Cardinals 45-21 Who have you beaten? Saints, Jets, Cardinals It’s not exactly a murderer’s row of wins for the Lions, beating up on teams that are a combined 4-11. But we knew going into this season that the Lions had one of the easiest schedules in the league, and they just need to take care of business against the bad teams. So far, they’ve done that, even if legitimate questions remain about Detroit’s defense. USA Today: 12 (Previous rank: 15) From Nate Davis : QB Jared Goff has accounted for 13 TDs and nary a turnover through five weeks. If that’s not MVP-caliber, then what is? CBS Sports: 12 (Previous rank: 20) From Pete Prisco : The offense continued to be good in the victory over the Cardinals, while the defense made strides. They got pressure up front, which helped the bad secondary. Sporting News: 13 (Previous rank: 18) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions realized they just need to go up big with offense to play better defense. Aidan Hutchinson and Alim McNeill each got into the pass-rush fun in the winning five-sack effort against the Cardinals. Yahoo Sports: 13 (Previous rank: 19) From Frank Schwab : The Lions’ defense is likely to still be a problem, even though it played well against the Cardinals. Detroit’s offense is just fine. Jared Goff has 12 touchdowns and no interceptions through five games, which puts him in rare company. But the engine of the offense is Jahmyr Gibbs. He leads the NFL with 747 yards from scrimmage and nine total touchdowns. That’s a pace of 30.6 touchdowns, in range to challenge LaDainian Tomlinson’s single-season record of 31. Gibbs didn’t deny he has eyes on that record. “Oh, yeah, for sure. Yeah, I’m trying,” Gibbs said, via MLive
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Lions vs Cardinals Song of the game: ‘Back on my BS’ by BigXthePlug
summary: Every single game in the NFL counts. It’s a big reason why the league is so popular, and why football season as a whole captivates all of us for five-plus months. At the same time, when you hear players and coaches speak about the early portions of the regular season, you hear a lot of […]
full_text: Every single game in the NFL counts. It’s a big reason why the league is so popular, and why football season as a whole captivates all of us for five-plus months. At the same time, when you hear players and coaches speak about the early portions of the regular season, you hear a lot of the same sentiments from around the league. “We are trying to establish an identity,” or, “You don’t really know who you are until about mid-October.” And for your 2026 Detroit Lions, that certainly appears to be the case. After a disappointing loss to the Carolina Panthers in Week 4, the Detroit Lions bounced back in a major way with a 45-21 thumping of the Arizona Cardinals in Week 5. The Lions’ defense took several steps forward, and after a slow start, the offense looked like a newly-evolved version of their former selves. You could almost say that they were back on their bs. I got paper, ain’t doin’ no stressin’, the one who put all this together They gave me somethin’ good and I made that s*** better Turnt up the notch, my watch changed up the weather I’m bigger and better, s*** bigger than ever At times, it looked like some of those games from the 2024 season when the Lions’ offense was just pouring it on against several overwhelmed opponents. At the same time, it looked different than some of those units from the past. Whether it is the MVP-caliber play from quarterback Jared Goff or running back Jahmyr Gibbs, the evolved version of wide receiver Jameson Williams, or how first-year offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is running the offense. It felt similar in the way they were dominating the Cardinal’s defense, even though it was being accomplished in a different manner. Like I mentioned at the top, it’s still early in the season with a long road to go. And while there have been ups-and-downs through the first five weeks, being 3-2 heading into their Week 6 bye is not a bad spot to be in. Especially with the lingering returns of safety Brian Branch and center Cade Mays. Enjoy this Victory Week, Lions fans. And maybe throw on some BigX while you do it. If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016 , 2017 , 2018 , 2019 , 2020 , 2021 , 2022 . And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here .
author: Morgan Cannon

title: Where every Detroit Lions starter ranks at their position at the bye
summary: The bye week is a perfect opportunity for some self reflection, and you better believe the Detroit Lions are doing that following their uneven 3-2 start to the season. With back-to-back division games out of the bye week, this is the perfect time for the team to reset, make some changes, and look a little […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-SEPTEMBER 27: Quarterback Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions leads the huddle during the first half of an NFL football game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 27, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The bye week is a perfect opportunity for some self reflection, and you better believe the Detroit Lions are doing that following their uneven 3-2 start to the season. With back-to-back division games out of the bye week, this is the perfect time for the team to reset, make some changes, and look a little unpredictable when welcoming the Green Bay Packers to Detroit in Week 7. While they do all of that, I figured this would be a good time to just check in on each individual starter and see how they’ve performed thus far. And to do that, I’m doing the very inexact analysis of looking at their PFF grades. Look, I don’t swear by these grades, which is why I’m also going to provide my own commentary based on my own personal perceptions. But it is a decent way to at least get a snapshot of how these players are playing and where they rank among the rest of the league. I don’t have time to watch every single game and every single player in the NFL, so this is about as good of any way to provide a league-wide view of Detroit’s start to the year, as long as we all agree PFF grades have their limitations. Quarterback Jared Goff 86.3 PFF grade, sixth in NFL Goff is off to a fantastic start, ranking second in passing yards, second in passing touchdowns, ninth in yards per attempt, and third in passer rating. Sixth seems a little low, but PFF’s grading system rewards mobile quarterbacks, so it’s not surprising to see Lamar Jackson, Bryce Young, Brock Purdy, Patrick Mahomes, and Joe Burrow ahead of Detorit. [Note: PFF’s No. 1 QB is Drew Lock, but I am excluding him since he only had one start.] Running back Jahmyr Gibbs 88.3 PFF grade, fourth in NFL Gibbs is currently fourth in rushing yards, t-first in rushing touchdowns, and first in receiving yards among running backs. I have no problem putting Gibbs fourth, currently behind Kenneth Walker, Bhayshul Tuten, and Bijan Robinson—especially since they’re all with 2.5 points. It’s worth noting Gibbs has the highest receiving grade (91.0) of any back. Tight ends Sam LaPorta 80.6 PFF grade, fourth in NFL Brock Wright 57.0 PFF grade, 55th in NFL (out of 81) It’s certainly relieving to see LaPorta establish himself as a top-tier tight end after a back injury ended his 2025 season early. LaPorta currently leads all tight ends with 316 yards, and is tied for fifth in touchdowns. And while his blocking continues to improve, he is comfortably out of the top-20 in both pass blocking (69.6, 28th) and run blocking (56.9, last) Wide receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown 73.6 PFF grade, 32nd in NFL (out of 114) Jameson Williams 62.5 PFF grade, 69th in NFL (out of 114) Isaac TeSlaa 59.3 PFF grade, 87th in NFL (out of 114) If there’s been a unit that has underwhelmed compared to expectations, it’s this one. St. Brown has still been very productive (12th in yards among WRs), but he’s had an odd amount of drops and fumbles. Jameson Williams remains a big-play machine, but he battles through some early drops. Isaac TeSlaa is starting to become a bigger part of the game plan, but started off slow. Offensive line LT Penei Sewell 90.9 PFF grade, 1st in NFL among all OT LG Christian Mahogany 86.4 PFF grade, 3rd in NFL among guards C Juice Scruggs 75.6 PFF grade, 1st in NFL among centers RG Tate Ratledge 75.5 PFF grade, 13th in NFL among guards RT Blake Miller 67.1 PFF grade, 33rd in NFL (out of 72) Wow. This is a bit surprising. The Lions have an outstanding offensive line by PFF standards, but that doesn’t quite match the eye test. Don’t get me wrong, this is a much-improved unit from last year, but the inconsistencies are obvious (and expected with such a young unit). Scruggs being the No. 1 graded center is shocking. He’s been good, but there have been a couple of down games. Perhaps this just says more about the current state of NFL centers. With no Frank Ragnow, Jason Kelce, Drew Dalman anymore, maybe the league just lacks good centers right now. The worst graded player is first-round rookie Blake Miller. But for him to be a middle-of-the-pack offensive tackle in his first five NFL games is more than acceptable. Defensive line EDGE Aidan Hutchinson 91.4 PFF grade, 2nd in NFL DT Alim McNeill 79.4 PFF grade, 9th in NFL DT Tyleik Williams 66.0 PFF grade, 40th in NFL out of 133 DT Skyler Gill-Howard 54.9 PFF grade, 83rd in NFL out of 133 EDGE DJ Wonnum 56.7 PFF grade, 79th in NFL out of 95 Alim McNeill is back. Aidan Hutchinson is still Him. Tyleik Williams has shown improvement. And then you have Wonnum’s puzzling grade after tallying 5.0 sacks through five games. He’s being dinged for poor run defense (40.5 grade), but I’m not so sure I agree with that. It’s maybe a little more apt for Gill-Howard (51.6), but that’s still not bad for a Day 3, undersized pick. Regardless, Detroit has to be pretty happy with this unit’s overall performance. Linebackers LB Jack Campbell 58.4 PFF grade, 52nd in NFL out of 72 LB Derrick Barnes 66.9 PFF grade, 28th in NFL LB Malcolm Rodriguez 78.3 PFF grade, 5th in NFL Campbell’s slow start has been a shock to the system, but hopefully he’s back on track after producing a 79.2 PFF grade against the Cardinals—13th best of any linebacker in Week 5. It’s encouraging to see Detroit’s other two “starting” linebackers put up decent numbers. And it looks like Rodriguez has earned more playing time despite only playing in 28% of snaps through five weeks. Cornerbacks CB D.J. Reed 66.3 PFF grade, 39th out of 104 CB Roger McCreary 53.8 PFF grade, 80th out of 104 CB Rock Ya-sin 42.4 PFF grade, 95th out of 104 CB Ennis Rakestraw 64.3 PFF grade, did not qualify Nothing about this is particularly surprising, although Reed was a bit higher than expected. He’s starting to turn his season around, after really struggling in man coverage through the first few games. The entire unit is being dragged down by coverage grades, because they’ve actually fared okay as run defenders. McCreary ranks 14th in run defense grade (78.9), while Reed isn’t far behind at 69.0. But McCreary is 94th in coverage grade (47.1), and Reed is 41st (64.6). Safeties S Chuck Clark 70.9 PFF grade, 23rd out of 95 S Christian Izien 63.3 PFF grade, 44th out of 95 S Avonte Maddox 38.9 PFF grade, 92nd out of 95 This doesn’t pass the eye test to me. Clark hasn’t been as reliable as advertised, and Izien has been far too inconsistent. For both to rank in the top half of safeties in the NFL just doesn’t look right to me. But perhaps it’s a sign that things aren’t as bad as they seem. In case you’re wondering, Keith Abney received a 59.9 PFF grade for his one start at safety against the Cardinals, dragged down by a 55.5 coverage grade. Overall By PFF grade, the Lions have top-10 players quarterback, running back, tight end, offensive tackle, both guards, center, defensive end and defensive tackle. Their players in the trenches are playing great, which should bode well for future success. Unsurprisingly, the weaknesses are in the back seven on defense. That said, the wide receiver room has a ton of room to grow, and there’s no reason to believe they won’t play better moving forward. One last thing to leave you on: PFF offers full-team grades, and the Lions currently rank first with an 85.0 grade. Their offense ranks first at 84.1, their defense is 13th at 67.4, and special teams ranks 16th at 76.9.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions stock report: 20 risers, 3 fallers against the Cardinals
summary: The Lions had us there for a minute. Three straight three-and-outs, with a sack allowed on each short possession while trailing 7-0 in Glendale, felt like the team was on the brink of its lowest point in the last two seasons. Then they triumphantly responded with a 31-0 run, including 24 points in the second […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Sam LaPorta #87 of the Detroit Lions celebrates after making a catch during the fourth quarter of the game against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. Lions 45-21. (Photo by Norm Hall/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Lions had us there for a minute. Three straight three-and-outs, with a sack allowed on each short possession while trailing 7-0 in Glendale, felt like the team was on the brink of its lowest point in the last two seasons. Then they triumphantly responded with a 31-0 run, including 24 points in the second quarter, and a total of seven straight scoring drives. It was the definition of a get-right game and a desert demolition of a team they should be dropping scoring at will against on the road. Dan Campbell’s team didn’t quite play a complete game, but it was chock-full of complementary football, just as he had challenged them to play throughout the week leading up to it It was a step in the right direction heading into the bye, before their first slate of divisional games immediately afterward. With that, the Week 5 stock report has its fair share of stock-ups as opposed to stock-downs. Stock up: Sam LaPorta, TE LaPorta, a key offensive cornerstone in a contract year, sure looked like the break-in-case-of-emergency player for the offense. Jared Goff called him the catalyst for everything and illuminated how his key plays changed the landscape of the game. LaPorta revved the team’s engine with a vital fourth-and-3 catch to move the chains for the first time all day on Detroit’s fourth possession, making a tight-window grab over the middle as he was clobbered by Mack Wilson Sr. It continued on the next drive, Detroit’s second touchdown drive, when he made rookie Wydett Williams Jr. miss to turn upfield on third-and-long and get to fourth-and-inches. He then set himself up on the very next play for a wide-open 38-yard gallivant into the end zone to pull ahead for the first time and for good. He also pulled off a twisting, diving grab down the seam for a first down in the fourth quarter and finished with five catches on five targets for a season-high 88 receiving yards, half of which came after the catch, while adding a few pivotal run blocks on the edge. It was a good reminder of why the offense’s consistency fell off after LaPorta’s injury last season. Stock up: Penei Sewell, LT In a game where the Lions got their groove back and dropped a forty-burger, it’s important to highlight their prize steer. Sewell, the best player on the team and one of the best players in the NFL, took a few lumps switching to Goff’s blind side but is quickly looking more natural with every snap he takes. For the second time in three games, Sewell didn’t allow a single pressure, this time on 34 dropbacks. Most fans wouldn’t have known Josh Sweat had even played, with Sewell clipping his pass-rush wings while also completely washing Zaven Collins and Jordan Burch on a handful of pass-protection reps. Sewell also continually put defenders on skates, driving them back, often on double teams with his new partner in crime, Christian Mahogany. He sealed the edge well and climbed to the linebackers to give Jahmyr Gibbs great running room to the left side, all while blocking through the whistle. A rare impact player at the position. Stock up: DJ Reed and Roger McCreary, CBs The Lions’ secondary has been the most criticized position group this season, having been questioned throughout the offseason, with seemingly none of the cornerbacks finding their comfort level or bearings in the first month of the season. Chief among the criticism as of late was 2025 high-priced free agent DJ Reed. Not without reason, as he hadn’t looked composed in man coverage or competent in zone coverage, and had struggled in the red zone and on deep passes. But Reed responded with vigor in possibly his best game as a Lion, and definitively his best of this season. I’ve questioned Reed’s run support, as he hadn’t reached the bar of what I believed he was capable of, but he was laying the wood against Arizona, including three tackles for loss on Jeremiyah Love. In coverage, Reed locked down Michael Wilson, with some safety help, allowing only four completions for 30 receiving yards, two first downs, just three yards after the catch, and a 67.6 passer rating on seven targets (all against Wilson). On the other side, McCreary made his third start for the Lions in his Amik Robertson-esque role as the second outside cornerback who shifts into the slot in nickel, and delivered his best performance as a Lion. With Detroit’s defensive approach focused on making the Cardinals play left-handed, shutting down the run, and allocating additional resources to Michael Wilson and Trey McBride, McCreary was tasked with covering all shapes and sizes of Arizona’s secondary receiving options. He was targeted an astounding 18 times but kept battling, producing a career-high six pass deflections while allowing seven first downs, including shutting out Jalen Brooks on five targets. With the Lions defense getting back to a little more man coverage, having their top two corners playing with confidence rather than being liabilities will go a long way toward getting this defense closer to the middle of the pack and giving the team a chance to maintain its title-contending aspirations. The real challenge will be the bombs away Packers offense in Week 7. Stock up: Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs, QB & RB One of the best backfield duos in all of football, Goff and Gibbs are both off to tremendous starts to the season, with each having the potential to enter the MVP or Offensive Player of the Year conversations, respectively, especially with the best supporting cast around them in the Dan Campbell era. Goff was aggressively heaving the ball with conviction, completing six passes of 10-plus air yards for a whopping 152 passing yards (25.3 yards per completion) and three touchdowns. He spread the ball evenly among his weapons while also quickly delivering catchable, YAC-friendly passes in what was Drew Petzing’s best-designed screen game of the season. Meanwhile, Gibbs was the other half of the two-headed monster that stirs the Lions’ drink, recording just the third 200-plus-yard game from scrimmage of his career and helping Detroit matriculate the ball downfield through both the ground and the air. Gibbs posted season highs in yards after contact (93, third-highest of his career), yards after contact per attempt (3.7), and rushing yards over expected (+49), while breaking off six runs of 10-plus yards (second-most this season). Gibbs also flashed in limited pass protection reps. Quick Hits STOCK UP: Christian Mahogany & Tate Ratledge, OGs: Becoming one of the better young guard duos in football, they were essential in generating push up the gut for Gibbs as the game wore on and are continuing to improve in pass protection, insulating Goff from the kind of interior pressure he suffered through last season. The two were charged with a total of just one quarterback pressure on the afternoon. Jameson Williams, WR: Red-zone weapon and deep-ball threat. Waymo made plays. Brock Wright, TE: I can be fairly critical of Wright as TE2 at times, but he kicked Cardinals defenders’ red tails in as a run blocker. Easily his best blocking effort of the season, and his 11-yard reception was his longest of the season (thanks to Williams occupying three defenders running deep). Sione Vaki, RB: Starting to become a valuable asset as a pass blocker, which may really come in handy against Brian Flores’ defense. Also recorded three special teams tackles. Aidan Hutchinson, DE: A slightly quieter game for Hutch, but it felt like the Cardinals made a more dedicated effort than any other opponent this year to get three or four hands on him just about every play, freeing up one-on-one opportunities for others. Hutchinson’s two consecutive plays early in the fourth quarter,…
author: Al Karsten

title: Discussion: What changes do the Detroit Lions need to make after their bye week?
summary: The Detroit Lions bye week is upon us after five weeks of up-and-down football. The team enters the break on a high after trouncing the Arizona Cardinals 45-21 on Sunday, but there is still room for improvement across the roster and coaching staff. The bye week is an opportunity to get healthy and get reinforcements, […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on during the fourth quarter against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions bye week is upon us after five weeks of up-and-down football. The team enters the break on a high after trouncing the Arizona Cardinals 45-21 on Sunday, but there is still room for improvement across the roster and coaching staff. The bye week is an opportunity to get healthy and get reinforcements, and the Lions will surely benefit from the return of Brian Branch and Cade Mays to the lineup, among others. However, the bye is also a time to reflect on what has and has not worked early in the season. An NFL season is a marathon and not a sprint, so any lessons they can take from their early slate of games can be used to improve down the stretch. What aspect of the Lions is in need of a change after the bye? Today’s Question of the Day is: What changes do you want to see from the Detroit Lions after their bye week? My answer: I want to see the offense be more efficient and effective in the first quarter. There is no shortage of improvements that Detroit needs to make. Their secondary needs to maintain the level of play they had versus the Cardinals. The linebackers need to improve in coverage, especially against tight ends. The team in general needs to clean up their execution and reduce their number of false starts, holds, delay of games, and illegal formation. One avenue that I think the Lions can and should improve upon is their first quarter scoring. Through five weeks, the Lions have scored an absurd 164 points, all without a defensive or special teams touchdown. Surprisingly, only 10 of those points have come in the first quarter. They scored a touchdown on their second drive versus the New Orleans Saints in Week 1. They were shut out against the Buffalo Bills and New York Jets in Weeks 2 and 3. They mustered a lone field goal against the Carolina Panthers in Week 4. Against the Cardinals in Week 5, they started with back-to-back-to-back three-and-outs. It is a testament to how good this offense can be that they are scoring this many points despite essentially punting away the first quarter. In contrast, the Lions have scored 57 points in the second quarter, 45 points in the third quarter, and 52 points in the fourth quarter and overtime—that is a staggering difference. What is causing the slow starts? Are crowds hyped up early in the game and causing poor communication? That is perhaps an answer for the Buffalo game, but Detroit has also had two home games, one of which featured their only first quarter touchdown. I would not say that travel is the cause. Neither would I say that chemistry or offensive scheme is the issue. Despite some shuffling of the offensive line, the blocking up front has been largely effective and cohesive, especially compared to 2025. As for play calling, Drew Petzing can clearly get the offense operating at an elite level, but for some reason it takes a quarter for things to start rolling. I think the recurring trend is a negative play causing the offense to stall: Versus the Saints, two of their first quarter drives ended in punts after suffering some type of loss: a loss of three on third-and-1 killed the first drive and the second was hampered by a holding penalty on first down. Versus the Bills, the Lions gave up two sacks and a botched snap on the first two drives. Versus the Jets, Jared Goff was again sacked twice over the opening pair of drives. Versus the Panthers, their first two drives stalled due to holding penalties on first down, though they managed to end the first drive with a field goal. Versus the Cardinals, Goff was sacked on each of the first three drives en route to a three-and-out. There is a very clear trend: if the Lions offense falls behind the sticks due to a negative play, whether self-inflicted or not, they sputter. Penalties should be correctable, but the Lions are being particularly hurt by sacks allowed. Across their five games this season, the Lions have only scored 10 points on a drive in which Goff was sacked: a field goal versus the Saints in the fourth quarter and a touchdown versus the Bills in the dying minutes of the game. Simply put, getting sacked early in the game is killing drives. The despite the sacks allowed, I think blame is not solely on the starting offensive line or Goff. There is a myriad of reasons why the sacks have been happening. Backup Larry Borom was on ice skates versus the Bills. Opponents have been springing well-timed blitzes. Routes have been slow to develop or simply smothered by good coverage. If the Lions offense can clean up their procedural mistakes and minimize these early-game stumbles, imagine how much more threatening this team could be. Though the defense played well versus Arizona, there is still a legitimate question about how effective they will be against better competition. One way to help out the defense is to keep them off the field for as long as possible. Another way to help out is to simply score early and score often. I think that the Lions offense has the ceiling to do both. What do you want to see the Lions clean up during the bye? Join the conversation. Join the conversation! title: Texans vs. Jaguars odds: Opening lines for Week 6 matchup
summary: The Houston Texans are fresh off their first victory of the 2026 season and are looking to build on that momentum against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. All three phases of the Texans were in sync this past weekend, and they dominated the Tennessee Titans from start to finish. Quarterback C.J. Stroud was throwing the […]
full_text: The Houston Texans are fresh off their first victory of the 2026 season and are looking to build on that momentum against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. All three phases of the Texans were in sync this past weekend, and they dominated the Tennessee Titans from start to finish. Quarterback C.J. Stroud was throwing the ball with a ton of confidence, which he has done throughout the season. He was able to make plays with his legs, extend plays when needed, and consistently put the offense in positions to succeed. Houston’s defense was dominant from start to finish. They made Titans quarterback Cam Ward’s life miserable, making it extremely difficult for him to establish any sort of consistent rhythm. This was DeMeco Ryans’ first game back calling plays for the defense, and the unit finally looked like what most expected entering the season. That defense needs to start stacking good performances, and the talent is absolutely there. The Texans have one of the most talented defensive units in football, but their inability to close out games has been a major reason for their disappointing start. If they can continue playing the way they did against Tennessee, this team has a legitimate opportunity to turn things around. The upcoming matchup against Jacksonville will not be easy, especially considering the Jaguars have been playing competitive football. Houston will need another complete performance on both sides of the ball if it wants to come away with its second consecutive victory. Texans vs. Jaguars: FanDuel Betting Odds According to FanDuel Sportsbook, the Texans enter this matchup as underdogs, meaning oddsmakers currently favor Jacksonville to come away with the victory. Despite that, Houston has plenty of reasons to feel confident heading into this matchup. Stroud has looked comfortable operating the offense, and the defense finally showed signs of returning to its dominant form. One of the biggest factors will be whether Houston can establish a consistent rushing attack and avoid putting Stroud in difficult situations. The Texans have the offensive weapons to make plays against Jacksonville, but they need to execute consistently throughout all four quarters. The Jaguars will certainly present a tougher challenge than Tennessee, and playing overseas adds another element to the matchup. For Houston, the formula is relatively simple. If the offense continues moving the football and the defense plays up to its potential, there is no reason the Texans cannot compete with Jacksonville. A victory would put Houston in a much better position moving forward, especially after starting the season with four consecutive losses. The Texans have plenty of ground to make up, but another win could go a long way toward getting this season back on track. Jacksonville enters Sunday’s matchup as a slight favorite, according to FanDuel Sportsbook. The Jaguars are currently 2.5-point favorites, with the over/under set at 42.5 points. The Texans are listed at +118 on the moneyline, while Jacksonville sits at -138. That tells you just how competitive this matchup is expected to be, despite the difference in the two teams’ records. Houston is coming off a dominant 26-3 victory over Tennessee, while Jacksonville enters the game at 4-1. The Jaguars have gotten off to a much better start, but the Texans have shown that they can compete with talented teams, even if the results have not always gone their way. This is also an AFC South matchup, making it even more important for Houston to come away with a victory. Falling further behind Jacksonville in the division standings would make an already difficult start to the season even harder to overcome. The Texans have the talent to win this football game, but they need to build on what they showed against Tennessee. If Stroud continues playing with confidence and the defense delivers another strong performance, Houston has a real opportunity to leave London with its second consecutive win. title: The Day After the Day After: Houston Texans bludgeon the Tennessee Titans 26-3
summary: The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 5 Much needed win? Yes. Season saved? Too early to call…: You didn’t need advanced analytics […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - OCTOBER 11: C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans celebrates with Nico Collins #12 after scoring a touchdown during the third quarter of the game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 5 Much needed win? Yes. Season saved? Too early to call…: You didn’t need advanced analytics to tell you that Houston was in a must-win situation. The odds at 0-4 are bad enough. 0-5…well, that would be uncharted territory. If it was the lowly Titans that effectively ended the dreams of a supposed contender barely a quarter of the way into a season, few outcomes could be more painful. Fortunately for Houston, they did what they had to, leaving Nashville with a resounding 26-3 victory. For one game, the team played defense like they envisioned coming into the season, holding the Titans to under 190 yards total offense, forcing 2 turnovers and allowing only 3 points. Yes, last season’s run was spurred by a 26-0 blasting of these same Titans. However, the circumstances are much different. Houston is now 1-4 vs. 1-3, and last season, two of those 2025 losses were to NFC teams. This season, 3 losses are to AFC squads. Also, three of the 2026 losses were at home. Last season, only one home loss in that 0-3 start. Tiebreakers helped Houston last year. They may hurt it this year. The running game is not alright: While Houston had a relatively stress-free win, there are still some significant issues. In particular, the running game is not even close to working on a majority of cylinders. The Titans do have some strength on the defensive interior, but for a “get right” game, the running game could not take advantage. This is the 4th straight game that Houston finished with less than 80 total yards rushing. The offseason offensive star acquisition David Montgomery only musted 11 yards on 5 carries before leaving the game with a groin injury, leaving his status as day-to-day. Marks at least managed over 4 yards a carry but only checked in with 62 rushing yards. For all the investments in the offensive line and running game, the Texans are not getting anywhere close to a good ROI. The subsequent trade for Marvin Harrison Jr post-game seems to indicate that Houston will lean into its passing game. If the defense could respond to its expected standard, that might win games. However, with a finishing stretch in December/January where Houston has to play at Pittsburgh, Washington D.C., Philadelphia and Green Bay, the lack of running game in inclement weather will prove a significant liability. Revenge Game for Tommy Townsend? Perhaps not: This offseason, Houston decided not to renew the contract for Tommy Townsend, who punted for the Texans for two seasons. Townsend, a Super Bowl winning punter from Kansas City, moved on to the Titans. Certainly, he might have enjoyed outkicking Kroeger in this matchup. While Townsend’s numbers were ok for a punter (4 punts/47.0 average/1 punt inside the 20), he didn’t exactly make Houston feel sorry that they moved on. Kai Kroeger’s line: 2 punts/37.5 average/2 punts inside the 20. Helps that Houston didn’t really need to call on Kroeger all that much, but on this day, Houston is likely happy that it saved some money on its punting. THE CRITICAL PLAY: 1st Qtr (8:24) TEN Ball at the TEN 14, 2nd and 9, Cam Ward incomplete pass deep left to Kylen Granson. On the opening drive, the Titans drove the ball into the Texans’ red zone, but the Houston defense stiffened, forcing a FG. On the subsequent drive, after forcing a Houston punt, the Titans looked to continue that momentum. On the second play of the drive, Ward dropped back and saw an open TE, Kylen Granson, deep left, with S Blankenship on the coverage. Ward was under some pressure, but he did have time to find the open man. The throw was just off the fingertips of the Titans’ TE. If he completes the pass, the Titans move up the field by about 20 yards. For a Houston defense that is among the league leaders in allowing explosive plays, this was a bad miss for the Titans. The Texans shut down the Titans on the subsequent 3rd Down, forcing a punt. Houston would score a tying FG on the next drive, and on the Titans’ next possession, Houston forced the first of two turnovers. Two drives after that missed completion, Houston is up 6-3, and the Titans would be unable to put additional pressure on the Texans’ defense the rest of the game. That incompletion was as much about momentum for the Texans and Titans. FUN WITH NUMBERS: 3: Most of Will Anderson Jr’s stats: Sunday’s game for Will Anderson was brought to you by the number 3. He had 3 solo tackles, 3 sacks, 3 TFLs and 3 QB hits. He was credited with 4 total tackles, and if you divide his jersey number (51) by 17, you get the number 3. What that last data point has to do with anything? Eh, why not? 8.4/77.6 : Average penalties/yards penalized per game by Houston: Sunday saw Houston commit 11 penalties for 95 yards. In the past two games, those numbers are 12/92.5. Didn’t hurt them this game, but those numbers go a long way towards explaining that now 1-4 start. GAME BALLS: QB CJ Stroud: With the aforementioned struggles with the running game, this offense is going as far as Stroud’s arm will take it. 26 of 34 for 261 yards and TD, while only taking 2 sacks and his 4th straight game sans a turnover will help that immensely. Only 5 yards rushing on 6 scrambles, but no one is perfect. LB Jake Hansen: With To’oTo’o still out and Al-Shaair just returning to the lineup, Hansen has been pressed into service to cover the LB2 spot. In this game, he did his part, with 6 tackles (3 solo), 1 TFL and 2 PDs. He did snag an INT, setting up a FG. While it was all due to the defensive line (thank you Danielle Hunter), Hansen was the right man at the right time. DEs Will Anderson/Danielle Hunter: 6 combined tackles, 4 combined sacks, 5 QB hits/pressures, forced an INT. That also helps out a defense. SHOULD BE FORCED TO LISTEN TO THE DRUNKEST BACHELORETTE PARTY DOING KARAYOKE ON MUSIC ROW ON REPEAT WHILE CLEANING UP SAID BARS IN THE HOURS AFTER LAST CALL: Titans Owner Amy Adams Strunk: Has it occurred to the Titans that maybe the whole “trying to troll the current Houston franchise by wearing the Columbia Blue” for their matchups in Nashville is just not working? 0-4 since 2023 when facing the Texans at home. Yes, they’ve incorporated the color into their everyday uniforms starting this season, but even ol’ K.S. Adams would’ve considered changing something here. Houston Texans’ run blocking . They can’t generate holes for running, and when the Texans do finally get a decent run play (aka Marks’ 24-yard run negated by a Brevin Jordan hold…and a needless one at that), they commit dumb penalties. Toro and the Terrible Towel: Bad Toro! Bad Toro! Steelers might not be what they once were, but those cursed towels…mess with them, they will mess back. 0-8 combined since tearing up said towel…sheesh. Houston is back in the win column, now sitting at 1-4. They will embark on their 3rd ever overseas trip to play the London Jacksonville Jaguars. Kickoff is at 8:30 a.m. CDT and broadcasting on the NFL Network. Set your alarms and see you there.

title: Not just Big Q: Colts have another standout offensive guard playing some elite ball
summary: We’re always searching for silver linings as the Indianapolis Colts sit at 2-3, but look closer to approaching a full blown rebuild than realistically contending for a Super Bowl title anytime soon. One of them is regarding the standout play so far of starting offensive lineman Matt Goncalves, the 3rd-year pro who just began his […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - JANUARY 04: Matt Goncalves #71 of the Indianapolis Colts steps up to block during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re always searching for silver linings as the Indianapolis Colts sit at 2-3, but look closer to approaching a full blown rebuild than realistically contending for a Super Bowl title anytime soon. One of them is regarding the standout play so far of starting offensive lineman Matt Goncalves, the 3rd-year pro who just began his second season as a full-time starter at right guard due to positional necessity. The former 2024 Colts’ 3rd round pick out of Pitt is blossoming into one of the better young starting offensive guards in all of football right before our very own eyes this 2026 season. While there was consensus concern among Colts fans that allowing breakout starting right guard Will Fries, who Indianapolis will face in two weeks, to leave in free agency to the Minnesota Vikings in the 2025 offseason, would prove to be a critical mistake in hindsight, Goncalves appears to have sufficiently filled those rather large shoes. Per PFF, Goncalves is their 12th best graded offensive guard with a +75.9 overall grade through 5 starts in the 2026 campaign. Specifically, he’s allowed just a sack and 3 total QB pressures so far in 195 total pass blocking snaps. His allowed pass pressure rate (5.7%) is among the best at his starting right guard position. If this keeps up, the big man, approaching 320 pounds, can chug as many footballs as he wants in celebration!
author: Luke Schultheis

title: ESPN writer believes Colts should play QB Anthony Richardson Sr.
summary: According to ESPN’s Ben Solak, the Indianapolis Colts, sitting at 2-3, should play primary backup quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr., given the underwhelming play of starter Daniel Jones through five games so far this season: I might think … the Colts should play Anthony Richardson Sr. They won’t trade him, and Daniel Jones looks like his […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 11: Anthony Richardson Sr. #5 of the Indianapolis Colts warms up prior to a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Ben Solak, the Indianapolis Colts, sitting at 2-3, should play primary backup quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr., given the underwhelming play of starter Daniel Jones through five games so far this season : I might think … the Colts should play Anthony Richardson Sr. They won’t trade him, and Daniel Jones looks like his arm is weaker almost every single week. This offense could really use an infusion of playmaking from a talented runner at the quarterback position. Interestingly enough, Solak stops short of saying that the Colts should actually start Richardson Sr., although given Jones’s physical limitations coming off a torn Achilles so far, maybe that’s implied here. I’m not saying I can’t eventually get there , if the Colts continue to play lackluster football, but I’m just not there yet. By giving up on Jones this early in the season, you essentially are waving the white flag that he’s not the QB answer either. You’d be creating a starting quarterback controversy again in Indianapolis, and the infamous saying by the legendary late John Madden is, “When you have two quarterbacks, you actually have none.” When the Colts re-signed Jones to a 2-year, potentially $100 million deal with incentives this past offseason, they had to know that Jones may not fully regain his physical form from the ‘first half of the 2025 campaign,’ until later this season or maybe not entirely at all until the 2027 season. The thought was always that 2026 may be a bit of a redshirt year regarding Jones’ recovery, which is perhaps why his representation pushed for a 2-year deal from the Colts—and received it. Coming off the Achilles tear, Jones hasn’t looked as physically explosive rushing the football outside the pocket and appears to not be stepping into his throws in the pocket as routinely, which has contributed to his noticeable lack of arm strength when throwing downfield. That being said, you have to play confident in the pocket to be successful at the pro level, so at a certain point, this cannot continue for the Colts to realistically make the playoffs. Jones has to play stronger in the pocket. When the best thing that Colts fans can say about Jones during last Sunday’s loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers is that “he didn’t turn the ball over,” that’s not exactly a ringing endorsement for a starting quarterback who’s 29-years-old and is firmly in the midst of Year 8 playing in the NFL. Jones may have not lost the Colts the game last weekend in Pittsburgh, but he didn’t win it for them by any means either. He’s not carrying this offense any time soon right now. If the Colts collectively continue to underwhelm, and Jones is consistently playing around average league starting quarterback play, neither hurting, nor helping the Colts win football games, at one point, would you consider pulling the lever for Richardson? Week 12? At that point, longtime general manager Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen are likely in the final fight for their jobs, and maybe, at that point, they’d heave a Hail Mary out of desperation? Turning to Richardson again to save their floundering season? At that point, you’d admit that Jones is not the starting quarterback answer here either, but if Steichen would lose his head coaching job in that situation regardless, what value does Jones even have coming back in 2027 without Steichen? In my opinion, a lot of Jones’ improved play and value to the Colts is tied to being paired with Steichen. If you take the latter out of the equation, does Jones even have value with a potential new coaching regime coming in? (It would be a $35.2 million 2027 dead cap hit the Colts would have to absorb either way, but without a 2027 first round pick and a lack of free agent quarterback upgrades, they may be tied to Jones for another year). These are all questions that have yet to be answered, but things should get clearer as the 2026 campaign progresses. However, Richardson returning to the Colts first-team offense as the starter over Jones isn’t quite as far-fetched as it once may have seemed only a few weeks ago, although nothing, and I MEAN NOTHING, appears imminent.

title: Colts’ Week 5 QB Analysis: Not Good, but Better
summary: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. […]
full_text: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) In Week 5, the Colts offense actually did a pretty good job of moving the ball downfield, but couldn’t finish drives, settling for field goals instead of touchdowns. The passing game was a major contributor to those struggles. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: arsr , edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , qbsr , epa/p , adj/p Indianapolis got a bit above average production from its running game while leaning heavily on the pass on early downs. ( 15th ARSR; 8th EDP ) Jones faced less than average pressure even though his time to throw was right about average, so that means the O-Line gave him decent protection. ( 21st PR%; 2oth TIP; 15th TTT ) The passing game took a dramatic turn downfield compared with last week. Jones had one of the deepest average target depths in the league, although his completed passes traveled much shorter distances with about average yards after the catch. ( 2nd ADOT; 14th AY/C; 15th YAC; 12th YD/C ) The deeper passing approach came with a major drop in completions. Jones completed just 57.1% of his adjusted passes (throwaways and drops removed), which was about the worst of any QB in week 5. A lot of that was 4th quarter desperation, but even after adjusting for depth, his accuracy was poor resulting in poor yardage efficiency (31st AC%; 24th CPOE; 25th AYPA ) Jones rarely scrambled or threw the ball away, and he took just one sack which helped preserve yardage when looking at all dropbacks. ( 29th SCR%; 25th TA%; 29th SCK% , 18th NY/D ) The passing offense struggled as Jones moved the chains on fewer than 30% of dropbacks and failed to produce a touchdown. ( 24th 1ST%; 30th TD% ) On the positive side, Jones avoided turnovers entirely, which helped offset some of the negatives. (24th TO% ) Overall, Jones was much more consistent than last week, with successful plays on 43.8% of his QB plays. But the offense still lacked enough productive plays to generate meaningful value. He finished just above zero in EPA per play, slightly below the league average. ( 18th QBSR; 21st EPA/P ) mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p Jones’ biggest problem this week was accuracy. Despite throwing much deeper than usual, his 57.1% adjusted rate pulled down his efficiency. That left him with very little production through the air, and the offense struggled to sustain drives. On the positive side, Jones avoided the costly mistakes that hurt him last week. He took 1 sack, didn’t turn the ball over, and produced a respectable rate of successful plays. But without more completions or explosive plays, that consistency wasn’t enough to generate much value. Jones actually had a pretty productive first half, generating several big positive plays and helping the Colts move the ball despite some inconsistency. But the 4th quarter was a different story. The passing game stalled, with incompletions piling up and very few meaningful gains. The Colts never recovered offensively, turning what had been a somewhat promising start into a disappointing finish. Jones bounced back a bit from his disastrous Week 4 performance, improving across all top four measures. His EPA per play returned to roughly league average, while his success rate, first-down rate, and net yards per play also recovered. However, all four measures remain at or below average, and the longer-term trend is still moving downward. Week 5 was an improvement, but Jones has yet to regain the promising form he showed last year. HOW FAR? Jones got off to a productive start, connecting on several passes that moved the chains and generating some meaningful gains through the air. But that production faded as the game went on. The second half was dominated by incompletions, particularly on deeper throws, and Jones struggled to sustain drives. Despite taking big shots downfield towards the end of the game, he rarely connected, leaving his yards per attempt steadily declining. Jones took a much more aggressive approach in Week 5, with his average depth of target jumping from just 3.8 yards to 11.5 yards, one of his highest marks over the past 17 weeks. However, his average depth of completion increased only modestly, from 3.7 to 6.1 yards. The large gap between the two means Jones was taking considerably more shots downfield but struggling to connect on them. Jones ranks near the bottom of the league in yards per attempt, averaging just 6.0 yards per throw off of shorter throws. TO WHO? Tyler Warren led the Colts’ receivers with 83 yards on seven catches, producing most of his yardage through the air. Keenan Allen and Josh Downs also contributed, with Downs generating almost all of his yardage before the catch. Laquon Treadwell was targeted eight times but managed just two receptions On the year, Downs leads the Colts in receiving yards, with Warren close behind. But they’re getting their production in very different ways. Downs generates most of his yardage through the air, while Warren relies much more heavily on yards after the catch. Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell are the next two contributors, with Treadwell’s production coming primarily on deeper completions. Jones pushed the ball farther downfield this week. Josh Downs and Laquon Treadwell all finished below average in EPA per target despite being targeted well beyond the league’s average depth. Tyler Warren was the notable exception, generating positive value on intermediate throws, which is what I have been waiting for all season. Downs and Pierce have been Jones’ most productive receivers in terms of EPA per target, both generating above-average value on deeper throws. Tyler Warren seeason totals are finally above average despite working primarily underneath. HOW ACCURATE? Jones’ accuracy took a big step backward in Week 5, with his adjusted completion rate falling to its lowest point in the last 17 weeks. He was particularly ineffective on throws over 20 yards, while his best results came on throws within five yards of the line. Even after accounting for the difficulty of his targets, his completion rate remained below expectations, continuing a troubling trend over the past several weeks. HOW FAST? Jones’ time to throw returned to roughly league average in Week 5 after being unusually quick the previous week (due to pressure). He also took only one sack, doing a good job of avoiding negative plays. His season-long numbers show that he’s getting the ball out faster than expected for the depth of his targets, which is a good thing. TO WHERE? Jones’ deep passing was pretty ineffective but his shots on the left side under 20 yards found success. Well, at least we have 2 green boxes now.

title: Colts promote Pharaoh Brown, re-sign Germaine Pratt to practice squad
summary: The Colts made two roster moves Tuesday, signing veteran tight end Pharaoh Brown to the 53-man roster and bringing linebacker Germaine Pratt back on the practice squad. Brown has spent the entire 2026 season on Indianapolis’ practice squad after rejoining the organization during training camp. The 32-year-old gives the Colts another experienced option at tight […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - JANUARY 04: Germaine Pratt #53 of the Indianapolis Colts drops back to block during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts made two roster moves Tuesday, signing veteran tight end Pharaoh Brown to the 53-man roster and bringing linebacker Germaine Pratt back on the practice squad. Brown has spent the entire 2026 season on Indianapolis’ practice squad after rejoining the organization during training camp. The 32-year-old gives the Colts another experienced option at tight end alongside Tyler Warren, Mo Alie-Cox and Drew Ogletree. Brown has appeared in 94 NFL games with 56 starts during stops with the Raiders, Browns, Texans, Patriots, Seahawks, Cardinals and Colts. He has 74 career receptions for 752 yards and three touchdowns. Brown also previously spent part of the 2023 offseason with Indianapolis before being released at the end of training camp. The more interesting move may be the return of Pratt. Pratt spent most of last season with the Colts after beginning the year in Las Vegas. He started 12 games for Indianapolis in 2025 and finished with 101 tackles, five tackles for loss, eight passes defended, an interception, a forced fumble and two fumble recoveries. The 30-year-old also has extensive familiarity with defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo. Pratt played his first six NFL seasons in Cincinnati from 2019-24, the same six seasons Anarumo served as the Bengals’ defensive coordinator. Across 112 career games, Pratt has made 104 starts and recorded 734 tackles, eight interceptions, eight forced fumbles and 33 passes defended. For now, Pratt joins the practice squad rather than the active roster, but the addition gives Indianapolis another experienced linebacker at a position that has been inconsistent and poor through the first five weeks. Akeem Davis-Gaither has handled the green dot and the majority of the MIKE linebacker snaps, while Jaylon Carlies, Bryce Boettcher, Austin Ajiake and rookie CJ Allen have filled out the rotation. Considering Pratt’s experience in Anarumo’s defense and his production for Indianapolis last season, he could give the Colts another option if the current linebacker group continues to struggle.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: The Colts got the Spencer Shrader decision right
summary: The Colts had one of the more unusual roster battles in the NFL this summer. Spencer Shrader and Blake Grupe were both good enough to be starting kickers. Grupe had been perfect for Indianapolis after joining the team late in 2025, making all 11 of his field-goal attempts and all 10 extra points, including a […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - OCTOBER 11: Spencer Shrader #3 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates with teammates after completing a 57 yard field goal in the first half of a game at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts had one of the more unusual roster battles in the NFL this summer. Spencer Shrader and Blake Grupe were both good enough to be starting kickers. Grupe had been perfect for Indianapolis after joining the team late in 2025, making all 11 of his field-goal attempts and all 10 extra points, including a franchise-record 60-yarder. Shrader, meanwhile, was returning from the torn ACL and MCL that ended what had also been an excellent 2025 season. Before the injury, he had made 13/14 field goals and all 14 extra points. There really was not an obvious wrong choice. Grupe was the more consistent kicker throughout much of training camp, while Shrader had some rough stretches. Once the games started, however, the competition flipped. Shrader went 5/5 during the preseason, including two field goals from at least 60 yards. Grupe finished 2/4. Special teams coordinator Brian Mason said at the time that game kicks would likely carry more weight when the final decision was made, and the Colts ultimately kept Shrader. Five games later, that decision looks excellent! Shrader is 16/16 on field goals this season, including 6/6 from beyond 50 yards. His only miss of any kind has been one extra point. He has the most makes of any kicker in the NFL and the most makes over 50 yards. Whether that makes him definitively the best kicker in football through five weeks is debatable, but there is not much of an argument that he belongs in that conversation. Last Sunday in Pittsburgh might have been his best performance yet. The Colts repeatedly moved the football before stalling in Steelers territory, and Shrader was basically their offense for large portions of the afternoon. He tied the franchise record with five field goals, opening the scoring from 57 yards and then drilling another from 56 later in the first quarter. He added makes from 22, 40 and 28 yards and finished responsible for 16 of Indianapolis’ 22 points. The 57- and 56-yarders are the ones that stand out. Those are not kicks where simply making them is expected. Shrader hit both in an outdoor road grass environment in Pittsburgh and made them look routine. There weren’t even close to missing. It follows a pattern we already saw during the preseason, and it is why I favored Shrader when the Colts had to make their decision. Kicking competitions remind me a lot of what you see on a golf driving range. There are plenty of golfers who can stand on the range and hit beautiful shot after beautiful shot. The lie is perfect, the target never changes and there is nothing riding on the result. Put that same golfer on the 18th tee with water down the right side and something actually on the line, and suddenly the swing can look completely different. Kicking is not exactly the same, but the pressure element is very comparable. Training-camp kicks obviously matter. You want consistency, and Grupe deserved a lot of credit for being the better kicker during stretches of the summer. The Colts also had to figure out which player they trusted when the operation was live, defenders were coming off the edge and the kick actually counted and Shrader kept answering that question. He did it during the preseason. He did it against Houston when he went 4-for-4 and hit the late field goal that won the game. Now he has gone into Pittsburgh and made five more, including two from well beyond 50 yards. That does not mean Grupe was a bad option. The difficult part about the competition was that Indianapolis probably had two NFL-caliber kickers and knew it would have to let one leave. Grupe had already shown the previous season that he could handle the job. The Colts simply picked the better one. At least through five games, Shrader has given them almost everything they could have asked for. He has range, has been perfect on field goals and has already delivered in important situations. In a season where Indianapolis has had plenty of problems elsewhere on the roster, kicker has become one of the positions nobody has to worry about.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Colts’ performances from Week 5 loss at Pittsburgh
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (2-3) fell to the Pittsburgh Steelers (3-2) on Sunday afternoon, 34-22, and the Horseshoe was simply outcoached, outplayed, and out-willed in a tough road environment where they haven’t won since 2008—with that franchise losing streak only continuing. Without dwelling on this latest loss, let’s take a look at some of the individual […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 11: Tyler Warren #84 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter of a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (2-3) fell to the Pittsburgh Steelers (3-2) on Sunday afternoon, 34-22, and the Horseshoe was simply outcoached, outplayed, and out-willed in a tough road environment where they haven’t won since 2008—with that franchise losing streak only continuing. Without dwelling on this latest loss, let’s take a look at some of the individual highlights and lowlights: Horsepower PK Spencer Shrader: The Colts returning kicker has been arguably their best player through 5 games, and made all 5 of his field goal attempts in Pittsburgh, tying a Horseshoe franchise single-game record. In inclement weather conditions, these weren’t easy kicks either by any means, as Shrader’s makes included longs of 57 and 56 yards. You hate to kick 5 field goals in any game instead of scoring touchdowns offensively, but he’s been a huge special teams asset and most notably, from long distance as of late. TE Tyler Warren: Colts head coach Shane Steichen finally was able to get Warren unleashed a bit, who led the Indianapolis offense with a team-high 7 receptions for 83 total receiving yards, as well as a 1-yard fullback touchdown run on 4th and goal near midway through the second quarter. CB Sauce Gardner: This could’ve been one of the big bragging points for Colts fans—had Indianapolis actually been road warriors and won on Sunday. Steelers wideout DK Metcalf inexplicably pretended to not know who Gardner was prior to the game when speaking to the media , and Gardner limited the former to just 1 reception on 2 targets for 9 total receiving yards when matched up opposite one another in coverage. Gardner clearly had a rough outing in London, but bounced back in Pittsburgh in a big way. Unfortunately, the Colts couldn’t make enough plays to land the W. Horseplay Run Blocking : The Colts are a ‘run-first’ team with star running back Jonathan Taylor rushing to set up the pass, but Pittsburgh kept both running backs in check holding Taylor to a paltry 3.0 ypc avg. on 15 carries and rookie backup Seth McGowan to 3.2 ypc avg. on 5 carries as a change-of-pace. The Colts had a very challenging time consistently running the football effectively, as the Pittsburgh front seven was clearly committed to shutting down #28 first and foremost as their top priority in tough weather conditions. Colts Defense: Whether it was Aaron Rodgers initially starting a perfect 10 for 10 in pass attempts, throwing for 3 passing touchdowns to 0 interceptions, or Steelers running back Jaylen Warren making NFL history on the ground and through the air , it was collectively a miserable showing by the Colts already much maligned defense. There was hardly any edge pressure yet again, as the Colts had just one sack, and the Indianapolis run defense was gashed, allowing a whopping 6.7 ypc avg. to Warren on 15 carries—with his 50-yard, 3rd quarter touchdown run clearly boosting that number. The Colts struggling linebackers can’t cover middle of the field in pass coverage, the Indy pass pressure isn’t nearly consistent enough, and the Colts corners give up too easy of short throws with provided cushion. To me, it’s both a coaching and personnel issue for the Colts defensively, and it’s a fair question of whether they have the horses and juice right now to actually get it solved in-season. I don’t want to hear anymore about a lack of effort or ‘want to’ regarding tackling. We’re already 5 games in. If it hasn’t happened already, when will it?
