title: Cleveland Browns gets their close-up in first trailer for Hulu's 'The Land'
summary: Created by Dan Fogelman, the NFL-backed drama follows a fictional version of the Browns and premieres the day after Super Bowl LXI.
full_text:
Even if the Cleveland Browns miss the NFL playoffs, fans will still have a chance to watch the team in February.

 The Browns are the focus of Hulu's upcoming scripted drama "The Land," which released its first trailer Tuesday ahead of its Feb. 15 premiere.

 Created by Dan Fogelman, whose credits include "This Is Us" and "Paradise," the series follows a fictional version of the Browns as the franchise navigates navigates challenges on and off the field.

 

 Christopher Meloni, best known for portraying Elliot Stabler on "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit," stars as Danny Roarke, Cleveland's head coach who is tasked with reviving the struggling franchise. With his job on the line, Roarke's best shot at turning things around rests on his own son, a rookie quarterback out of Ohio State .

 The fictional quarterback, Connor Roarke, already had his NFL draft moment earlier this year.

 Ahead of the second day of the 2026 NFL draft in Pittsburgh, commissioner Roger Goodell took the stage to announce a surprise selection .

 "With the first pick of the 2026 NFL draft, the Cleveland Browns select Connor Roarke, quarterback, Ohio State," Goodell said.

 Of course, the announcement was part of filming for the series, not an actual draft selection.

 

 Meanwhile, William H. Macy plays the Browns' owner, Hal Durkin, who faces a different kind of competition as he decides which of his two daughters will take over the franchise.

 "It's about a football team, nominally the Cleveland Browns," Macy told Deadline in January. "They're brilliant scripts. They're Shakespearean. It's about football, but, oh, my lord, the plots are so profound, and I'm having the time of my life."

 The cast also includes Mandy Moore, Chace Crawford, Sam Corlett, Tanner Zagarino, Chloe Bennet, Bridget Moynahan and Omar Epps.

 With the NFL serving as a co-producer, the series will feature authentic league branding and access.

 "The NFL is completely behind our show, so we've got complete access," Macy told Deadline. "I'm optimistic it's going to be something. And what if Cleveland starts winning? Because I think our team is going to do better."

 "The Land" premieres the day after Super Bowl LXI, with its promotional tagline promising, "When the game is over, the real drama begins."

title: Why the Browns' run game is at the root of their offensive struggles
summary: Cleveland's O-line hasn't been able to open running lanes consistently enough for Quinshon Judkins and others.
full_text:
One of Todd Monken's greatest strengths as an offensive mind has fallen short through five games as the Cleveland Browns ' head coach.

 The architect of punishing and explosive run games at both the college and pro levels, it hasn't translated early on in Cleveland. Those struggles were further evident in Sunday's 17-12 loss to the New York Jets , when the Browns accumulated a season-low 198 yards of offense.

 After quarterback Deshaun Watson was sacked a season-high eight times, Monken highlighted issues on the ground as the source of the Browns' continued offensive struggles.

 "You're going to put yourself in that position when you can't run the football," Monken said. "We weren't able to run the football [Sunday], and we were behind the sticks the whole day, and we made a few plays, some get back on track and some third downs that gave us a chance, but we were never comfortable calling it or playing, and that's not a recipe for success. Everybody knows that, but we got to be able to run the football to control the game. It starts up front, starts with the way we call it and the way we scheme it."

 

 When Monken took the job as the Browns' coach , he didn't adopt the plethora of blue-chip offensive linemen that he had at Georgia or the dynamic backfield he had with Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry with the Baltimore Ravens . However, there was optimism between second-round pick Quinshon Judkins , who led all rookies in rushing in 2025 before a late-season leg injury, the dual-threat capabilities of Watson and a new-look offensive line that included a mix of accomplished veterans and highly touted rookies.

 The vision of Cleveland's dominant run game, though, has failed to materialize in the first quarter of the NFL season.

 The Browns rank 21st in rushing yards per game (94.2) and 23rd in rushing yards per carry (3.7). A significant portion of that production has come from designed runs and scrambles by Watson, whose 167 rushing yards make up more than one-third of Cleveland's rushing total.

 Judkins, who leads the team with 221 rushing yards, is averaging 3 yards per carry this season, 39th out of 41 qualified running backs. The only players averaging fewer yards per rush are the Green Bay Packers ' MarShawn Lloyd (2.8) and the Houston Texans ' David Montgomery (2.7). Judkins is also averaging 1.14 yards per rush before first contact this season, by far the lowest of the 41 qualified running backs ( Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty is second at 1.23).

 After 100-yard rushing efforts in back-to-back games in Weeks 3 and 4, Cleveland's running game regressed against the Jets. The Browns totaled 96 yards on the ground, and Watson (40 rushing yards) almost matched Judkins' rushing total (44 yards).

 

 "It's never just one thing," Monken said Monday. "It's scheming. It's us running off the football. It's executing at a much higher level than we are right now. And until we do that, we will struggle. And it really wasn't that way at Pittsburgh [in Week 4]. I felt like we had made some strides, and the Jets have a good front, and we just didn't execute and certainly didn't coach it well enough."

 Up front, the Browns' offensive line hasn't been able to open running lanes consistently enough for Judkins and other rushers. The unit ranks 26th in ESPN's run block win rate metric (71.1%), which measures the proportion of plays in which a player "won" his block on designed running plays. Early-down struggles have also contributed to unmanageable third-and-long situations. Cleveland is 25th in yards per rush on first down (3.5), part of the reason that the offense is averaging 9 yards of distance to convert for a first down, the sixth-highest mark in the league.

 The Browns are also becoming a predictable offense when it comes to their rushing tendencies. Cleveland has increasingly been operating its offense out of shotgun; 76.2% of its plays come from a shotgun alignment, and 65.7% of its run plays are out of shotgun, both league-high rates. As more NFL teams are returning to under-center plays and taking advantage of its unpredictability in the run game, the Browns have just 30 designed runs with their running backs from under center, by far the fewest in the league. They haven't had much success on those attempts, averaging a league-low 1.9 yards per carry.

 "There's a little of everything that goes with it," Monken said of the offensive tendencies. "I mean, certainly we're capable of pivoting what we feel like is best for us moving forward. There's more to it than just that. But we were playing Tampa four weeks ago, we were under center, and they were pressuring us, and then we got in the gun and we had some success, and we were running it and we're throwing it, we're getting the ball out of his hands.

 

 "And each week you're pivoting. You want to have enough in your offense to not be pigeonholed as to one way to be able to move the football. And it's not in stone, it's in sand. And we're going to do what we feel like we need to do, even moving forward. Did we see that coming the other day? No. But that's what you do. You learn from it, you own it, you fight like hell to fix it, and you move on."

 Efforts to improve the running game could be dealt with a blow, as Judkins is day-to-day with an ankle injury he sustained against the Jets. Running back Dylan Sampson , who entered the season as Cleveland's No. 2 back, has missed the past four games on injured reserve because of a knee injury. Monken said it is a "possibility" the team will open his practice window this week.

 Despite the paltry rushing numbers, left guard Zion Johnson said there have been positive moments to build on.

 "In the run game we definitely had certain plays where we're one specific thing away from having the play we want, but it's not all negative," Johnson said. "We looked at it today from a blocking standpoint and from the way our running backs were running, there was a lot of good too and a lot of potential that we can really untap just by being more detailed. But like I said, our goal is fix the Browns hurting Browns, be more detailed and just continue to improve week to week. We know if we continue to do that, we'll be right where we want to be."

title: Broncos offense searching for more big plays, ready for Bo Nix to 'let it rip'
summary: Changing playcallers wasn't an immediate fix for the Broncos' offense, which still suffers from a lack of big plays and a QB who hasn't found his rhythm.
full_text:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. -- In the moments following a tooth-grinding escape against the winless Los Angeles Chargers , Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton talked about his continued wrestling match with time.

 The Broncos hope to slightly slow quarterback Bo Nix 's internal clock between the snap and the whistle to end each play. And they feel like succeeding with that adjustment would cause everything to fall into place for Nix and the Denver offense so they can, in Payton's words, "let it rip."

 "There's a lot that's been said about his feet, I think he's settling that down," Payton said in the moments after Sunday's 23-17 victory over the 0-5 Chargers. "[But] I think it's important from a protection standpoint we provide that early in game so that clock doesn't get juiced up a little bit."

 The Broncos moved to 3-2 with the victory, but it was not a smooth operation for the offense in its first game since Payton re-assumed playcalling duties . Denver finished 1-of-12 on third down against the Chargers, gained only 224 net yards and had one play longer than 12 yards before the fourth quarter. Nix finished with the second-lowest passing yardage of his career (16-of-27 passing for 123 yards and a touchdown).

 

 Following Sunday's games, Nix is 24th in the league in QBR (43.1) and 30th in completion percentage over expectation (minus-4.1%), ahead of only Cleveland's Deshaun Watson . The Broncos find themselves near the bottom of the league in most statistical categories on offense, including scoring (29th, 18.0 points per game). Only the Arizona Cardinals have fewer plays of 20 yards or more than the Broncos' 11.

 These struggles are part of why Payton snatched playcalling duties back from offensive coordinator Davis Webb after four games. But Payton's playcalling return saw many of the same issues that prompted him to make the change. And a coach who has made his résumé on a brash, go-for-it boldness spoke of the benefit of "small steps" for the QB as the Broncos' defense once again fueled a fourth-quarter comeback win.

 "Thought guys up front settled in," Payton said. "... And when we needed it, [Nix] gave us some important ones."

 Much of the outside angst about Denver's offense has centered on the 26-year-old quarterback's play. Many former QBs, including ESPN analyst Chase Daniel, who played for Payton in New Orleans, have spoken of Nix's footwork and his penchant for moving through his progressions too quickly before Broncos receivers are into their routes enough to be targets.

 Payton has acknowledged some of that, saying that he wants "make [Nix's] job easier" with a better run-game approach and improved pass protection, especially early in games, to get the QB settled faster. That mindset was apparent Sunday, which was the first game this season in which the Broncos had more rushing attempts than pass attempts.

 Though the Broncos rushed for fewer than 4 yards per carry on their 29 attempts (106 yards for 3.7 per carry), Payton said he believes the rhythm of the run game is important in helping Nix play with a little more freedom. Nix, who had two ankle surgeries this past offseason, has run less this season, and his 5.7 air yards per attempt currently ranks last among the league's 31 qualifying quarterbacks.

 "I think after [five] weeks there's a handful of things collectively, it starts with me, where it's like 'alright, where it's let's focus on the details' and I think the by-product helps the [quarterback]," Payton said. "I think the hardest thing to do in this league is play that position if you're not rushing the ball."

 

 Payton said he and the Broncos coaches have assured Nix that he's "the guy we want here." Nix has also acknowledged that he has tried to not press when things aren't going smoothly and that he, too, wants to find the let-it-rip zone.

 "When a coach says 'let it rip,' it means play what you see, have good vision, and I think there's just, right now, there's just a little subtle piece that's overall offensive execution that we're still working toward," Nix said. "Because at times it's there and at times, for whatever reason, the drive stalls."

 When the Broncos selected Nix with the 12th overall pick in 2024, Payton said it was in large part due to Nix's "superpower" -- his ability to avoid sacks and turnovers. But Nix has fumbled four times this season, including twice on Sunday, one which he lost. Nix knows he must be more careful before truly being able to let loose.

 "Letting it rip is one of the best things that you can do as a quarterback," Nix said. "At the same time, you've got to sort of earn that right. When you do the preparation, you earn the right to react so that you can let it rip."

 Things don't get any easier this week. The Broncos have a short week before a Thursday night game against the 3-2 Seattle Seahawks , the defending Super Bowl champions. Seattle is ninth in scoring defense and has surrendered the fewest yards per play in the NFL (4.2). The Seahawks are also tied for fourth in the league in quick pressures, which will challenge Nix's ability to slow down his internal clock.

 "[Hall of Fame coach] Bill [Parcells] taught me one thing and it's on going, if you're not having the output you're looking for, you have to look at reducing the variables," Payton said. "And we're trying to do that, reduce the variables so guys can play faster."

title: Packers' Watson-Golden WR combo reminiscent of Nelson-Cobb
summary: It has been more than a decade since Green Bay had a dominant WR duo, but Watson and Golden are making their mark.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- It's time to insert Christian Watson into the conversation of best receivers in the NFL. And while you're at it, throw Matthew Golden into talk about the most improved player in the NFL.

 Together, they have a chance to be the Green Bay Packers ' most productive receiver combination since the days of Jordy Nelson and Randall Cobb more than a decade ago.

 As dominant as Davante Adams was when he led the Packers in receiving every season from 2017 to 2021, he never had a consistent running mate.

 In Sunday's much-needed 31-7 win over the Chicago Bears , Watson and Golden showed why the Packers wanted to streamline their receiver room and give quarterback  Jordan Love a few go-to guys rather than a smorgasbord of receivers, none of whom ranked among the league's best. Jayden Reed was supposed to be part of the go-to group, but the Packers lost him for the season to a neck injury in Week 2.

 

 Against the Bears, Watson (six catches for 143 yards and two touchdowns) and Golden (six catches for 123 yards) became the first pair of Packers to each record 100 yards receiving in the same game since Adams and Marquez Valdes-Scantling did in 2021 against the Minnesota Vikings .

 "We talked about it a little bit last week, how good the offense can be. It just shows right there," Love said. "Those are two guys that are dominant factors. We get flowing like this and they're making plays and we're able to take advantage of what the defense is doing. Both those guys, they're capable of doing great things. I think that's just a little bit of, show what's possible."

 What's possible is this: Watson is on pace for 1,600 yards and Golden for nearly 1,350. The Packers haven't had a pair of 1,000-yard receivers in the same season since Nelson and Cobb in 2014.

 

 "Well, we'll see," coach Matt LaFleur said. "You're only as good as your last game. They were pretty good this week."

 Or as Packers safety Xavier McKinney said when asked how tough it would be for defenses to cover Watson and Golden if they play like that: "It's different."

 McKinney should know. He has had to do it in practice all year.

 "You see the speed," McKinney said. "I'm sure the DBs on the other side, they feel that speed. And when you've got a quarterback like [Love], I've seen it now for a couple years, so I know what he's capable of doing. I've seen the throws that he's made. I know the throws that he can make consistently.

 "Then obviously you get talented guys like C-Wat, M.G., [tight end] Tuck Kraft  ... once they start to get really clicking and really going, it's going to be a scary sight to see for any team."

 Watson, who had parts of the past two seasons impacted by injuries, ranks fifth in the league in receiving yards with 474 and second in touchdowns with six (behind Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba 's seven). Golden, with 24 catches for 397 yards, has already surpassed his yardage total from last season, when he was a first-round rookie, and is five catches behind his total.

 The numbers tell only part of the story. The film shows the other. How many receivers in the league can haul in the 53-yard touchdown that Watson did in the third quarter against the Bears? He reached over Bears safety Dillon Thieneman , who was giving chase, and then made sure the catch survived the ground after Thieneman knocked him down and sent him sliding toward the back of the end zone.

 

 "Honestly, I was kind of joking around with some of the guys after, that's just one of those ones that you watch it back on tape, and you're like, 'The DB should've broken it up or it should've been incomplete,'" Watson said. "Sometimes, you just find a way. I was just tracking the ball. I wasn't thinking too much. Just go get it and came down with it."

 Golden did much the same. On his 36-yard catch in the third quarter and his 50-yarder in the fourth, Golden had to go up in the air and twist his body to make the grabs.

 

 "It's hard to stop two guys who can run all the routes and stretch the field like that," Watson said of him and Golden. "If you try to, it's going to give us other opportunities elsewhere. Obviously we've got Tucker Kraft and we've got a lot of guys who can make plays. It's just tough when you've got playmakers of the ability we have in our room and our offense, to stop it all."

 The Packers can't expect to throw it deep with as much success as they did against the Bears. There's a reason Love had more completions on passes with 20-plus air yards (six) on Sunday than he did in the first four games combined (five): They're typically low-percentage throws that teams cannot count on week in and week out.

 "You can't, but it's OK," McKinney said. "We'll get [running back  Josh Jacobs] back soon, and we'll be OK. I think that even the backs now, the guys that are playing, have done a great job of making sure they're running hard and getting the extra yards, whatever the case may be, so it can open up the pass game. But when we get [Jacobs] back, yeah, it's gonna really show."

title: Marvin Harrison Jr. latest in Texans' quest to solve their WR2 conundrum
summary: Houston has traded and drafted receivers, hoping to complement No. 1 wideout Nico Collins and QB C.J. Stroud.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Trading for  Marvin Harrison Jr . falls right in line with how the Houston Texans  continue to attack the wide receiver room: aggressively.

 The organization has made ample investment into the receiving corps to try to elevate quarterback C.J. Stroud  and complement it's No. 1 wideout  Nico Collins , but coach DeMeco Ryans insists that the move (trading a second-rounder and sixth-rounder to the Arizona Cardinals ) was just to improve the Texans (1-4).

 "Each year, you just look at the team and you see where you are," Ryans said. "With myself and [general manager] Nick Caserio, it's, 'How can we always improve the team?' That's always the goal for us.

 "If it happens to just be the wide receiver room, maybe not by design that way, but it's like, 'Hey, what's available, what are we willing to give up in terms of getting a player and what does that player offer for us?'"

 

 Adding Harrison is the latest move to improve the wideout room since Ryans and Stroud arrived in 2023. The Texans took a big swing in 2024 when they acquired four-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Stefon Diggs  from the Buffalo Bills  for a second-round pick. Pairing Stroud with Diggs was promising, as he was on pace to eclipse 1,000 receiving yards, but he suffered a season-ending torn ACL in Week 8.

 The Texans did not re-sign Diggs, and they tried to replace him by acquiring Christian Kirk  from the Jacksonville Jaguars in the 2025 offseason. However, Kirk had a career-low 239 receiving yards in his lone season in Houston. And in late August, Houston acquired wide receiver Kayshon Boutte from the New England Patriots  for safety Jaylen Reed and a seventh-round pick in an attempt to find help after losing wide receiver Jayden Higgins , who tore an ACL during joint practices with the Las Vegas Raiders . 

 Higgins was coming off an up-and-down rookie season but was beginning to flash during camp and was projected to be the No. 2 wideout alongside Collins. Boutte is fifth on the team in receiving yards (153) with zero touchdowns despite being second in routes run (130) through five games.

 Besides drafting Higgins with their first pick in 2025 (a second-rounder), the Texans have used third-round picks on Tank Dell  (2023) and Jaylin Noel  (2025) and sixth-rounders on Xavier Hutchinson  (2023) and Lewis Bond  (2026).

 Now, they've added Harrison, who was the No. 4 pick in the 2024 draft, with a smiling Ryans announcing the trade moments after the Texans got their first win of the season Sunday.

 "We're excited to add Marvin Harrison Jr. to our team," Ryans said Monday. "He's another really great playmaker. He's crushed a lot of college records. Got multiple thousand-yard receiving seasons in college. All-American, always been a top receiver when he's been on the field. He has good rapport with [Stroud] from their time at Ohio State. We're excited to get him in, add another great player to our group."

 Harrison hasn't lived up to the bullish draft hype after his decorated college career. He has had 1,578 receiving yards and 13 touchdowns in 33 NFL games. 

 

 Stroud, teammates with Harrison in 2021 and 2022, was a driving force behind the move, so Houston is hoping reuniting the pair can help rejuvenate Harrison's career. 

 "He's probably the hardest worker I've ever been around in my life," Stroud said. "And then just who he is off the field. He's a great dude, quiet guy, but definitely, you feel his presence. I'm just excited to get him in here, to get him learning, and get him around other guys. And I think it's perfect for him."

 Though Ryans said the Texans haven't necessarily targeted pass catchers, the move marks the fifth time they've traded for a wide receiver since 2023, the most of any team during that stretch, according to ESPN Research.

 "It's a look at it from our perspective of, 'Can you improve the team?'" Ryans said. "Each year, whatever that looks like, wherever we are, each year is different."

 The years might be different, but Collins has been the constant. He has gone over the 1,000-yard-receiving mark in each year of Ryans' tenure. As far as the No. 2 wide receiver, Dell's 709 yards in 2023 still stands as the next-best season they've had.

 So, can Harrison eventually be the WR2 they've been seeking? Only time will tell.

title: Jaguars WR Parker Washington has the clutch gene: Will that earn him an extension?
summary: Did you see Washington's one-handed grab in London? How did he get so good at contested catches? And how did he quickly become a big part of the Jaguars' offense?
full_text:
LONDON -- Facing a fourth-and-5 from the  Philadelphia  27-yard line, the Jacksonville Jaguars got the look they wanted from the Eagles' defense. So, receiver  Parker Washington knew quarterback  Trevor Lawrence was going to throw him the football.

 Washington got a clean release off the line of scrimmage but then had to fight through contact with Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen , so he didn't see the ball in the air at first. As he got closer to the goal line, though, he finally picked it up.

 "As soon as I saw it, I was like, 'OK, there we go,'" he said.

 Washington reached out with his right hand, grabbed the ball and pulled it into his body while falling backward into the end zone. That gave the Jaguars the lead with little more than three minutes left in the fourth quarter, and they eventually won 19-17 on  Cam Little 's walk-off 57-yard field goal at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday.

 There we go, indeed.

 

 That sequence isn't anything unusual for the 2023 sixth-round pick, who has been one of the league's most clutch receivers since Week 11 of 2025. Over that span, Washington has 17 catches for a league-high 381 yards on third and fourth downs; his 22.4 yards per catch there is the best in the NFL of any player with double-digit catches.

 The foundation for Washington's proficiency began long before he even started school, and it has helped him play as if he's 6-foot-4 despite being 5-foot-10 with 29-inch arms. As the Jaguars' 2026 leader in catches (25), receiving yards (352) and receiving TDs (four), he is well on his way to a contract extension that could pay him more than $30 million annually as one of the NFL's top-paid receivers.

 "We consider him an elite wide receiver," Lawrence said. "I don't know what everybody else thinks, but we feel like he's pretty freaking good."

 
 How Washington mastered contested catches 
 The aggressiveness to make every catch is innate, but Washington's expanded catch radius developed as a result of a game he played with his father, Christopher, beginning at 3 years old and continuing through college.

 "One thing me and my dad used to do, he would grab -- it would be anything, piece of balled-up paper, wrap tape around a piece of paper or something like that -- and he would [throw it to him and] say, 'Catch it with your eyes,'" Washington said. "And what I would do, I would literally catch it with my eyes and sometimes the paper would hit me with my face or whatever. So it was just a game, but it was fun.

 "But little did I know, we were really training."

 Washington's training eventually evolved into normal football drills, workouts and tape study as he got older. The summer before his freshman year at William B. Travis High School in Richmond, Texas, it also became an early-morning routine -- something that continues with the Jaguars.

 Washington is regularly one of the first people inside the Jaguars' facility every morning. He was getting there just before 5 a.m. during training camp, grabbing a quick FaceTime call with his trainer to prep for the day's workout. Washington even joked he needed the passcode to turn on the lights.

 In his final two seasons at Travis High, Washington caught 124 passes for 2,315 yards and 35 touchdowns, and he joined  Penn State  as a four-start prospect. Nittany Lions receivers coach Taylor Stubblefield said he was impressed with how quickly Washington picked up the offense. He finished second on the team in receptions (36), receiving yards (489) and receiving touchdowns (six) as a true freshman in 2020.

 

 Stubblefield said Washington's extended catch radius and ability to make contested catches showed up quickly. Washington flashed the latter ability repeatedly throughout his four-year college career, even when it was snowing in a 2021 loss to  Michigan State .

 "When the quarterback [ Sean Clifford ] threw it, you're like, 'OK, that's an overthrow,'" said Stubblefield of one play from that game. "And he somehow climbed not one ladder, but two ladders, to go up and high-point that ball."

 A detail that Stubblefield left out: Washington caught it with one hand. Then with less than a minute left, he made another clutch, contested grab for a touchdown.

 Stubblefield, who is now the receivers coach at  Air Force , said Washington makes those kinds of catches because he has a strong lower body -- "He's built like a running back," he said -- and elite body control.

 "Sometimes if somebody has bad body control or they're not judging the defense right, they are off balance, which then they might not have full explosion," Stubblefield said. "They're not in a position to be able to maximize that explosion, and Parker does a great job of that, which helps his catch rate be so large for somebody who doesn't necessarily have the measurables for it."

 
 Washington's ascension with the Jaguars 
 When the Jaguars drafted Washington with the No. 185 pick in 2023, they intended for him to learn behind Christian Kirk , who was coming off the best season of his career (84 catches for 1,108 yards and eight touchdowns) for a year or two. So, while Washington played sparingly early in his first season, Kirk, Zay Jones and Jamal Agnew  sat out a combined 19 games in 2023. That pressed Washington into a bigger role, and he responded with 16 catches for 132 yards and two touchdowns, including an acrobatic catch in the back of the end zone on "Monday Night Football"  against the  Cincinnati Bengals  in Week 13.

 The same routine of filling in for injured players continued in 2024, as Kirk, Gabe Davis and tight end Evan Engram all sat out time. It happened again in 2025, when injuries to receivers Brian Thomas Jr . and Travis Hunter essentially made Washington the team's No. 1 receiver. That's when he stuck to the starting lineup.

 Washington caught 58 passes for 847 yards and five touchdowns, and he topped 100 receiving yards in three of the Jaguars' final four games last season (including the playoffs). Among those catches was a slider against the New York Jets on a ball that Lawrence threw while rolling to his left.

 

 Since the start of the 2025 season, Washington has 80 catches for 1,199 yards and nine touchdowns. His last catch was the one-hander against the Eagles, further proof to Lawrence that -- other than throwing the ball into the stands -- there isn't a spot he can put a ball where Washington won't catch it.

 "I think if it's in his vicinity, he's shown that he can make just about any play," Lawrence said. "And I think that's a cool thing as a quarterback to have that trust in a guy to where ... you get a one-on-one with him and just put it near him, and he goes and makes an unbelievable play."

 Coach Liam Coen, who has been with Washington for only 23 games, acknowledged that he has seen Washington make so many difficult catches that it sometimes dulls the "wow" factor.

 "I mean, you're amazed because of the moment and because of how big of a time it was, but to look back and to continue to see this guy make plays for our team, especially in some of these critical moments, it just speaks to the dude and to make critical plays and critical moments, he's showing that he can step up and do that stuff," he said.

 
 What could Washington's contract extension look like? 
 The Jaguars have wanted to extend Washington, who is in the final year of his rookie contract (four years, $4 million), since the 2025 season ended. But the sides  could not come to an agreement on annual compensation before the season began.

 The team has not closed the door on in-season negotiations, and is not afraid to make those types of decisions -- wide receiver  Jakobi Meyers and offensive tackle  Cole Van Lanen both received extensions during the 2025 season. But with each passing week, impressive performance and contested catch, the price for a new deal certainly isn't going down.

 Arizona's Michael Wilson has had comparable production to Washington since the start of last…

title: Jacksonville Jaguars remain in the NFL hunt thanks to Foyesade Oluokun's bone-crunching efforts
summary: Runaway AFC South leaders the Jacksonville Jaguars continued their impressive start to the season, with Nigerian-American linebacker Foyesade Oluokun starring in a 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles.
full_text:
Runaway AFC South leaders the Jacksonville Jaguars continued their impressive start to the season, with Nigerian-American linebacker Foyesade Oluokun starring in a 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles .

 Week 5 was a week in which many of the best performances from players with ties to Africa came from those who ultimately narrowly ended up on losing teams.

 

 Zimbabwe's Nate Landman (LA Rams) was up there with Oluokun for defensive impact in a 37-34 loss to the Buffalo Bills . Jaxon Smith-Njigba , who has proudly repped Sierra Leone on his helmet, was another prime example of an unlucky star performer, as the Seattle Seahawks went down 32-29 to the San Francisco 49ers .

 However, the Niners themselves benefitted from standout performances from two players with Nigerian ties -- Malik Mustapha and Osa Odighizuwa .

 African Player of the Week: Foyesade Oluokun (Jacksonville Jaguars) 
 The son of Nigerian parents, Oluokun has been instrumental in the Jaguars' success so far this season -- an understated but important part in one of the league's best defenses. In week 5, he starred with 10 tackles, including six solo and one for a loss, in the win over the Eagles.

 One could argue that Oluokun did not produce as many spectacular standout moments this week as the likes of Landman on defense and Smith-Njigba on offense and was fortunate to end up on the winning side when his main competitors for this week's award did not win their respective games.

 However, a counter to that would be that the often unseen steady contribution that Oluokun makes week-in-week-out is probably worthy of more accolades than he gets. In a sense, this Player of the Week prize could be seen as overdue recognition for a sturdy contribution over the course of five games -- four of which have seen the Jaguars come out on the winning side.

 

 African Moment of the Week: Jaxon Smith-Njigba (Seattle Seahawks) 
 Smith-Njigba -- of Sierra Leonean descent through his grandparents in a family with deep, complex West African ties -- weaved his way through four nearby Niners bodies to score a 16-yard catch-and-run touchdown off a Sam Darnold pass in the third quarter against the Niners, handing the defending Super Bowl champions the lead.

 The Seahawks may eventually have gone down in a narrow fight, but their star wide receiver was impactful as usual. He tallied 118 total yards, including 102 yards across five receptions.

 He did, it must be acknowledged, have a costly drop towards the end of the game. However, a bad moment towards the end of the game does not completely cancel out a memorable moment earlier - no matter how used to his brilliance we have become.

 With a record of 3-2 across the first five games, the defending champions can be forgiven for showing signs of growing pains, but as long as JSN is on board and on song, they cannot be written off.

 

 Honorable Mentions 
 The Niners' win over the Seahawks included major plays from Nigerian-American duo Osa Odighizuwa and Malik Mustapha, with the latter in particular having a game to remember with five solo tackles out of seven total, one fumble reception and one pass defended.

 The Nigerian missile was one of the key reasons why Smith-Njigba was unable to turn the game in the Seahawks' favor, making life tremendously difficult for the reigning Offensive Player of the Year in the decisive stages.

 One could make a case for Mustapha for Player of the Week based on high-intensity impactful moments alone, and the same could be said of the LA Rams' Landman - though he ended up on the losing side for the Rams against the Bills.

 Landman has become a master at the art of the punchout and forced two fumbles, making 13 tackles in a huge performance.

 The Tampa Bay Buccaneers ' win over the Dallas Cowboys saw big plays from Emeka Egbuka (of Nigerian descent) on offense and YaYa Diaby (of Guinean descent) on defense.

 Boye Mafe (Nigerian heritage) picked up a sack and a forced fumble for the Cincinnati Bengals in their 31-24 win over the Miami Dolphins .

 Sam Kamara , who has ties to Sierra Leone, picked up a first career sack - but in defeat as the Cleveland Browns went down 17-12 to the New York Jets .

 African-born Player Watch 
 Landman was the standout African-born player in Week 5, but Nigeria's Samson Ebukam notched up a sack in the Atlanta Falcons ' 30-23 loss to the Baltimore Ravens .

 Born in Onitsha, on the banks of the Niger River, Ebukam is on a tremendous run this season with 2.5 sacks in the last 3 games - half a sack against the Carolina Panthers followed by one apiece against the Baltimore Ravens and New Orleans Saints .

 The Falcons will, on Sunday, face a Chicago Bears side brimming with talented players with African ties. Kyle Monangai , who is of Cameroonian heritage, looks set to miss out through injury but Ebukam is likely to face Rome Odunze , who is of Nigerian descent through his father's side.

title: Dolphins not worried about young roster getting discouraged by losses
summary: Miami coach Jeff Hafley doesn't believe his players will grow discouraged by the lack of results so far this season.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Five games into the 2026 season, it's been no secret the Miami Dolphins are the youngest team in the NFL. At some point, that stops being an excuse.

 The Dolphins dropped to 0-5 after Sunday's 31-24 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals , during which they cut an 18-point fourth-quarter deficit to seven points but failed to recover an onside kick to extend the game. Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis threw for 137 yards and a touchdown, with a season-high 74 rushing yards and a touchdown -- but he threw two interceptions in the first half and lost a fumble, and Cincinnati scored 10 points off those turnovers.

 Willis was critical of Miami's offensive performance after the game and insisted that the team's inexperience doesn't make up for a lack of execution or accountability.

 "All we can do is put it out the best we can, and continue to try to keep that better than it was the week before," he said. "And it is too much and too hard to keep saying, 'Oh, we're just young. Oh, we're trying to build this and build that.' At the same time, we've got to hold each other accountable because we can't keep doing this to ourselves.

 "If we're going to be in games versus good teams, we've got to be able to take advantage of it and go and win those games -- because there's no point to be in the game if you can't go and win."

 Miami's 10 active rookies played a combined 455 snaps Sunday, and that's without Caleb Douglas , Kyle Louis and Trey Moore , who are all expected to play significant roles when healthy.

 First-year coach Jeff Hafley said last week that the Dolphins have "a lot of young guys in the huddle who don't have experience playing," but added that he expects improvement every week. One third of the way through the season, Hafley said the training wheels are off for his team, and he expects everyone to produce.

 "I want to see more consistency. I want to see better execution," he said Sunday. "I want to see the same fight. I want to see the same energy. I want to see the same connection. 

 The Dolphins have played the NFL's third-hardest schedule through five weeks. Sunday's game was their first against a team that wasn't undefeated. But their past three games -- against the Chiefs, Vikings and Bengals -- have all been one-score contests in the fourth quarter.

 Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez said after last week's loss to the Minnesota Vikings that Miami still needed to learn how to win. Entering its bye week in Week 6, Willis said a focal point this week will be identifying how to start fast and how to execute in critical moments.

 "I think we just got to watch the tape and figure it out," he said. "And that's the thing that I think Coach Haf does great. He holds everybody accountable and he's honest with us. If we need to do better, we need to do better. And if we got to execute, we need to execute. We got to figure out a way to get guys on the same page because there's just a lot left out on the field that could be better than what it is.

 "We try to find a way at the end, but that's just too hard to continue to try to fight back at the end."

 The Dolphins return from the bye to face the New York Jets in Week 7 in one of the most winnable remaining games on their schedule according to ESPN Analytics.

 Hafley said the team will debrief from Sunday's game, as usual, before starting its prep for the Jets. He doesn't believe his players will grow discouraged by the lack of results, and believes the Dolphins are "building" an identity centered around physicality and effort.

 "It's just (what we have been saying since) day one. It's who we are," he said. "It's what we have to be. We got really good guys. I don't even think that's going to be an issue."

title: The Saints' offense keeps declining each week. Can they turn it around?
summary: After dropping three straight games at home, New Orleans goes on the road with intent to turn things around.
full_text:
METAIRIE, La. -- The New Orleans Saints ' offense has endured nine straight quarters of misery in their home stadium this season.

 Coach Kellen Moore, starting quarterback Tyler Shough and all the Saints are hoping they can hit the reset button on the road the next two weeks.

 New Orleans (1-4) will travel to face the New York Giants on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ) and then will take on the Pittsburgh Steelers in France on Oct. 25 ( 9:30 a.m. ET, NFL Network ).

 At this point, it's difficult to know what the international crowd will get in the NFL's first game in Paris.

 Will fans see the Saints team that sparked hope with its second-half play against the Detroit Lions and Baltimore Ravens in Weeks 1 and 2? Or will they see the product that Saints center Erik McCoy said has "hit a sputtering block" in the past three games?

 "I think it's pretty blunt. S---ty performance wise," McCoy said following the Saints' 23-13 Week 5 loss to the Minnesota Vikings .

 

 Wide receiver Devaughn Vele said that afternoon that the offense wasn't on the same page against the Vikings.

 "There's just certain looks that we expected ended up being different looks. Guys are thinking different things. Obviously Shough was on a different page as well," the Saints wideout said. "This was a whole team effort."

 McCoy said things have been going wrong ever since the Week 3 loss  at home to the Las Vegas Raiders , and the team's statistics reflect that sentiment. The Saints have been trending downward in both points and yards in each loss.

 New Orleans had hoped to spark life into the Caesars Superdome with its recent three-game homestand, but each attempt has turned out worse than the last.

 On Oct. 5, the organization honored its 2006 team on the 20th anniversary of the return to the Superdome after Hurricane Katrina, while the current team lost 45-24 to the rival Atlanta Falcons in primetime. Then in Week 5, the Saints inducted former quarterback Drew Brees into their ring of honor at halftime of the Vikings game but went on to lose by 10 points in a game that would have been a blowout if not for two defensive takeaways.

 Saints owner Gayle Benson said Tuesday it was "truly disappointing" to lose to the Falcons in a game that was meant to celebrate the 2006 team. She also mentioned Brees' ROH induction and how the team should honor his legacy by upholding the standards he set. It was a rare critical comment by Benson that highlighted the disappointment of those losses.

 In speaking about the home loss to Minnesota, McCoy said the Saints' problems are an "all-around issue." The Saints consistently turn the ball over, start slow and commit penalties that put them behind the sticks.

 New Orleans has turned the ball over eight times since the fourth quarter of the Week 3 loss to the Raiders. The Saints have rushed for 55 yards or less in their past two games, and against the Vikings, they passed for only 96 yards. They rank No. 9 in the league in penalties counted against them but 24th in pre-snap penalties.

 Shough has been hit on 36 of his dropbacks this season, which is tied for third most in the league. He has also been playing with an injured non-throwing hand that requires wearing a protective layer at the moment. Shough has been handing off with his other hand and cannot use the injured hand to help himself off the ground.

 Moore would not confirm if Shough's hand is broken but said "he's doing OK."

 "It's kind of like a day-to-day thing. That felt like the easiest path for this week and we'll see how it goes. I think he came out of it feeling pretty clean, and so some soreness there and we'll go from there," Moore said.

 

 Shough had a career-worst performance as a starter against the Vikings in passing yards and passer rating, while throwing two interceptions and rushing for only 9 yards. But Vele said the team fully believes in the QB's ability to rebound.

 "He's got the right mindset," Vele said. "... As an offensive unit, we trust him with all our hearts. I know he's going to bounce back from this. I mean, it's on all of us. It's not just on Tyler. You know what I mean? This is a team sport."

 If the Saints are looking for immediate offensive help, they won't get any until after their Week 8 bye. The Saints waived running backs Devin Neal and Audric Estime earlier in the season with injury settlements, and Travis Etienne Jr . went on injured reserve with a hamstring issue in Week 4, meaning he'll be out until at least after the bye week. Left tackle  Kelvin Banks Jr . is out indefinitely after having ankle surgery in Week 3. Rookie first-round pick Jordyn Tyson , who has not played this season , will not return to practice this week and is likely a post-bye returner as well.

 Without the hope of an offensive spark, the Saints will have to regroup in the next two weeks. While the Saints are tied with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) for the worst NFC South record, they have time to turn things around with the Carolina Panthers leading the division at 2-2.

 Several players have said they believe they can do that, but it'll take more than just belief to make it happen.

 "We took a step in the wrong direction, I would say today, but it's not a matter of, like I said last week, we need to completely flip the script and we need to just change who we are," Shough said. "No, it's not that at all. And I'm going to continue to elevate how we prepare as an offense and how we continue to go. And that starts with me too, but by no means is there a matter of we need to cuss people out, do things like that. I mean, we need to continue to do what we're doing from that process and we have the right people in the building."
